title: Goldman trims forecast gains in South African rand.
text:
LONDON, July 12 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs cut its forecasts for how much the South African rand will strengthen against the dollar over the next 12 months, according to its latest client note.  

 The U.S. investment bank said it continued to recommend investors maintain short dollar positions against the rand but cut its forecasts to 6.7 rand in three months, 6.4 in six months and 6.7 in 12 months from its previous forecasts of 6.30, 6.25 and 6.40 respectively.  

 The rand stood at 6.7975/8075 per dollar at 0950 GMT.  

 The relatively peaceful outcome of elections in Zimbabwe and signs that South African inflation would shortly be peaking were seen as rand supportive.  

 But Goldman said it expected rand strength to be capped by the likely intervention of the South Africa Reserve Bank to reduce its forward book.  

 The central bank's net open foreign exchange position (NOFP) - which measures its uncovered exposure to the forward foreign exchange market - fell to $10.1 billion in June from $10.2 billion in May.  

 Goldman Sachs expects the central bank to hold the repo rate at 11.75 percent for the rest of this year and sees further easing in the second quarter of next year.  

 It saw this coming amid a significant decline in inflation as the effect of higher oil prices and this year's currency correction dissipated and the positive benefits of structural reform dominated.  

 The bank maintained its forecast of 12.8 percent yield on the R150 bond for the end of 2000 and 12 percent by mid-2001. It was yielding around 13.25 percent on Wednesday.  

 ((London Capital Markets, +44 20 7542 6176, andy.reierson@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX - Currencies  hit new highs, new lows.
text:
LONDON, March 6 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel and Slovak crown broke through new levels on Monday as investment flows pushed currencies ever higher while the rand hit an 18-month low against the dollar, echoing weakness in the local bond market. 

 The shekel broke through 4.0 to the dollar and was trading at 3.9997 bid at 1430 GMT, after hitting its highest levels since October 1998. 

 "It's heading for a very key level around 3.99 because the turning point between a possible bounce and a continuance downwards," said one trader. "If it breaks 3.99 it should continue to around 3.95." 

 He said the market was waiting to see what the Nasdaq would do after making strong gains on Friday. 

 "There is a kind of umbilical cord between the two. If the Nasdaq does shoot above the 5,000 level we'll see the Shekel gain ground," the trader said. 

 The Nasdaq opened unchanged. 

 The Slovak crown pushed ahead to its highest levels against the euro since the euro's birth, trading at 41.62 compared to Friday's close of 41.75, helped by positive sentiment on the country's outlook. 

 "We like the economy - there's an improving current account performance and lots of state asset sales in the pipeline. There are good reasons for the improvement in the crown," said Tim Ash, economist at WestLB. 

 Ash said the market was now trying to find a level after the central bank stopped intervening at 42.3 to the euro. 

 In South Africa the rand was telling a different story, hitting lows against the dollar not seen for the last 18 months, at 6.48 compared to Friday's close of 6.45. 

 "Fundamentally there's nothing that's been driving this. News has been very encouraging," said Razia Khan at Standard Chartered. She said the central bank had lost some credibility last week when it said its inflation targeting policy had been a bit rushed, though it is still likely to meet the targets. 

 With no major data due out in the next week for South Africa and investors also shunning the bond market, there is little to change the current situation, Khan said. 

 "Until we see a real recovery in the euro it is unlikely the rand will strengthen much against the dollar. But if you take into account the movements against the currencies of all South Africa's trading partners, in real terms the rand has been holding up strongly." 

 (Caroline Smith, London Capital Markets, +44 171 542 6414, caroline.smith@reuters.com). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Cbank  intervention  seen restraining S.Africa rand.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Dec 3 (Reuters) - South Africa's currency is expected to hold steady in coming weeks, economists say, but lurking central bank intervention will stop it strengthening as much as it could. 

 Over the past six months, the rand has held comfortably to a band between 6.00 and 6.20 to the dollar, with only brief spikes out of the range. Any strengthening through six has quickly been followed by a move back towards 6.10. 

 In its quarterly economic bulletin, released on Thursday, the Reserve Bank revealed one major reason for the pattern. 

 "The appreciation in the weighted effective value of the rand could have gone further...had it not been for the Reserve Bank's steady purchases of foreign currency," the December edition of the bulletin said. Earlier in the day, more information emerged on how much foreign currency the central bank has been buying. 

 Releasing November reserves data, the Bank said its net open foreign exchange position (NOFP) - its uncovered exposure to fluctuations in the foreign exchange market - declined by $900 million on the month to $14 billion. 

 The numbers were encouraging, and came on the back of a healthy decline in the NOFP (and forward book) in recent months, from $18.3 billion in June this year. 

INTERVENTION HOLDS BACK RAND 

 While economists are pleased with the reduction in a liability that makes foreign investors wary and has negative implications for interest rates, it is also holding up the rand. 

 "A base has been formed under the rand, it should be stronger - somewhere closer to 5.80 than 6.15," said Colen Garrow, economist at ABN-Amro in Johannesburg. 

 "But while the rand may not have reached its full potential, the forward book has come down a lot and that's encouraging from several points of view. (Reserve Bank Governor) Tito Mboweni is hell bent on getting the forward book down and he's doing it." 

 Garrow reckons the Bank will continue siphoning dollars out of the market as long as the currency holds between six and 6.25 and for as long as capital inflows to local securities give the currency fundamental support. 

 "As foreigners show interest in the equity market and, to a lesser extent, the bond market, the Bank will take dollars out...we're likely to see the currency around 6.10 in the run up to the budget (in February) rather than 5.90 or below." 

 Some currency traders are concerned the central bank's unspecified intervention floor could prompt speculators, who had a bash at the currency last year, to have another go. 

 But most think the Bank's policy will just prevent the rand from moving too close to six to the dollar and that foreign buying of local assets will prevent weakness on the other side. 

 "They're just taking dollars out very calmly, in a very orderly way. The rand is basically rangebound and steady," said one senior trader. 

 With the currency seen stable, and bonds and equities expected to get a boost from fresh capital flows after the millennium, the risk on the horizon may come with the budget. 

 Economists say that if Finance Minister Trevor Manuel decides to loosen exchange controls further, as everyone is clamouring for him to do, there would likely be a period of rand weakness as currency leaves the country. 

 ((Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 775 3131, fax +27 11 775 3132, email newsroom@reuters.co.za)).

title: S.Africa cbank says no comment on  fx intervention .
text:
JOHANNESBURG, June 22 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of South Africa on Tuesday declined to comment on market speculation it had taken advantage of the rampant rand to purchase dollars and unwind its heavy exposure in the forward forex market. 

 Bertus van Zyl, general manager of foreign exchange trading, told Reuters the Bank's policy of permitting two-way volatility in the currency remained intact. 

 This, he said, allowed it to buy small amounts of either rand or dollars from time to time, depending on the circumstances. But he declined to be drawn on specifics. 

 Analysts reckon the bank should sell rand for dollars in order to trim its hefty oversold forward dollar position, which stood at $22.2 billion rand at the end of May. 

 They also say the rand's resurgence - it has jumped to its strongest levels since early February in celebration of the country's peaceful June 2 election - is damaging the country's fragile exports and that the Bank would prefer to see it weaken. 

 South African export earnings have been pressured by the slump in bullion prices to a fresh 20-year low of $258 per ounce and would benefit from a weaker rand, which would make goods made here cheaper in foreign markets. 

 The rand has been boosted by dollar selling after traders said offshore hedge funds cut the long-dollar positions they had established ahead of the elections in anticipation of rand weakness. 

 With such a strong inflow of the U.S. currency into the market, dealers say it would be natural for the central bank to take advantage by soaking up the extra liquidity. 

 ((Johannesburg newsroom, +27-11-775-3131, 

 fax: +27-11-775-3132, e-mail: newsroom@reuters.co.za)).

title: Medium term prospects bearish for rand - Warburg.
text:
LONDON, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The medium term prospects for the rand are poor, although the short term outlook, buyoed by further interest rate cuts among G7 countries, is more favourable, analysts at Warburg Dillon Read said. 

 "With the rand now at levels reflecting overvaluation ... and with the possibility of the economy only running sustained current account surpluses in the next five years at the earliest, the rand remains vulnerable to further bouts of turbulence," analyst Mansoor Mohi-uddin wrote in a client note published on Friday. 

 Warburg said the rand would fall to 7.00 per dollar by the end of 1999, after rising from a low of 6.84 to the dollar in late August to a recent 3-1/2 month high of 5.48 as hedge funds and proprietary desks have closed out long dollar positions. 

South Africa's central bank has held back from intervening to cap the rand's gains, allowing it to strengthen. 

 "In the short term, we believe that the absence of leveraged players/proprietary desks and the further prospect of G7 interest rate cuts will provide further near term support for the rand," Warburg said. 

 But looking further ahead: 

 "While national elections in 1999 and the appointment of a new governor to the SARB are less likely to provoke currency turbulence...the 'reliquification' of global markets by U.S. interest rate cuts will enable leveraged players in the medium term to target more liquid emerging market currencies once again." 

 Warburg said the outlook for South African government debt was likely to be similar. 

 While bond yields may fall over the following three months: "over a one-year time horizon, bouts of currency turbulence are likely to reflect in yields periodically spiking higher again, and pre-crisis highs in the bond market, when yields fell to 12.4 percent, look out of reach." 

 ((Carolyn Cohn, London newsroom +44 171 542 6320, uk.forex.news@reuters.com)).

title: PRESS DIGEST - South Africa - Sept 25.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 25 (Reuters) - These are the leading stories in the South African press on Friday. 

 Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy. 

 - - - - 

 BUSINESS DAY 

 - The rand firmed against the dollar last night, accompanied by a firmer gold price, as Japanese and Hong Kong stock prices surged on Thursday. 

 - Voicing faith in Deputy President Thabo Mbeki's "assertive leadership" and government's commitment to prudent fiscal and monetary policy, US credit rating agency Duff & Phelps said it saw no reason to downgrade South Africa's long-term foreign currency and rand debt from BBB-and A-respectively, and declared the outlook "stable". 

 - The Federal Reserve Bank in New York has co-ordinated a 3.5 billion dollar baleout of one of the largest U.S. hedge funds, following fears that a collapse could worsen the contagion in financial markets. 

 - The Financial and Fiscal Commission, the body charged with advising government on provincial finances, is worried that government is stalling the devolution of taxation powers to the provinces. 

 - The Food and Allied Workers' Union (Fawu), racked by claims of financial irregularities, is unable to pay staff salaries this month. 

 - - - - 

 BUSINESS REPORT 

 - South Africa's vehicle manufacturers were owed an estimated 1.5 billion rand by the government for taxes paid in lieu of export benefits that should have been tax free, Roger Pitot, a consultant to the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa (Naamsa), said on Wednesday. 

 - The Russian central bank called for tough price controls on Thursday, warning that without prompt action inflation could explode to between 400 percent and 450 percent by the end of the year. 

 - Eskom, the state electricity utility, was expected to pump 40 million rand to 60 million rand annually into Esmed, its medical aid scheme, a top Eskom source said on Thursday. Esmed was not expected to break even in the next four years. 

 - A bitter row between the Council for Nuclear Safety (CNS) and the department of minerals and energy over radiation safety in mines had to do with money rather than safety, senior government and industry sources said this week. 

 - - - - 

 THE STAR 

 - As an uneasy calm returned to a devastated Maseru on Thursday after three days of looting and mayhem, President Nelson Mandela angrily described criticism of South Africa's military intervention in Lesotho as "ignorance". 

 - Cultural diversity was the theme of Thursday's Heritage Day festivities as South Africans celebrated with prayer, dance and song. 

 - It's get-away weather for those who want to get out and about this weekend, with the Weather Bureau predicting that most of Gauteng will be fine but partly cloudy. 

 - - - - 

 THE CITIZEN 

 - The voluntary removal from Fourways High School, Johannesburg of four girls accused of involvement in tuckshop thefts to totalling 48,000 rand was "tantamount to expulsion", governing body chairman Mike Hogan said on Thursday. 

 - A planned rolling protest by organised agriculture against farm killings has drawn support from a wide spectrum of other organisations and could turn into a mass demonstration against crime and the government's handling of it.

title: IMF praises as well as chides S.Africa - finmin.
text:
CAPE TOWN, Sept 9 (Reuters) - South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday an annual review of the country's economy by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had praised as well as criticised financial policy. 

 Manuel told a news conference the Cabinet had noted the report issued last week, which he said was positive on the progress South Africa had made in controlling expenditure in its provinces. He said the IMF was also content with the country's tight monetary and fiscal policy and financial sector regulation. 

 "There were a number of headings where it was indicated that these issues were being dealt with adequately," he said. 

 The report was particularly encouraging on South Africa's performance in regulating the financial sector and banking supervision, which was particularly important in the wake of banking crises in South East Asia, Manuel said. 

 The finance minister admitted that the Washington-based agency had taken South Africa to task over central bank intervention in the forward market to support the rand earlier this year and inadequate labour market flexibility. 

 The IMF report said South Africa had been wrong to intervene to protect the rand and should in future raise interest rates instead. The agency said South Africa's "uneven monetary policy" coupled with buying the rand on the currency markets had expose the economy to greater risk. 

 The rand came under heavy selling pressure in May as other emerging market economies suffered devaluations in the wake of last year's financial crisis that engulfed Asian countries. 

 Official interest rates in South Africa have surged to 21.855 percent from 15 percent in April as the central bank defended the rand from speculators who have robbed the currency of 25 percent of its value against the dollar. 

 The IMF said South Africa should close all its forward market operations run by the central bank, linked to its currency intervention, and urgently adopt a comprehensive policy response to restore market confidence in the currency. 

 This should include keeping a tight monetary policy, refraining from currency intervention, achieving its 1998/99 fiscal year budget targets and accelerating previously announced economic reforms, it said. 

 The finance minister said the document would become a basis of engagement at the forthcoming IMF annual meeting. 

 "You take these points, but it doesn't mean that there is an absolute correctness because it comes from the IMF," Manuel said. "We would reserve the right to take decisions as a sovereign member of the IMF and differ with them." 

 Manuel said Cabinet had also improved the draft Insider Trading Bill which aims to improve monitoring, investigation and penalties of irregular share dealing and said the legislation should be passed early next year. 

 ((-Emma Thomasson, Parliamentary newsroom +27 21 4032502 reutercp@iafrica.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: S.Africa markets face rough ride after IMF critique.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 2 (Reuters) - South Africa's bruised financial markets faced another rough ride on Thursday after a damning report on the country's foreign exchange policy from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 The Washington-based agency said on Wednesday that South Africa had been wrong to intervene to protect its battered rand and should in future raise interest rates instead. 

 "I think the markets will take it quite badly tomorrow morning when they wake up to this IMF report," said Mike Schussler, an economist at FBC Merchant Bank in Johannesburg. 

 "It's very unfortunate that the IMF would come out with a statement criticising South Africa's policy when the general consumer is in danger of falling over." 

 South Africa's economy has been reeling from a four-month currency crisis that has seen interest rates raised to the highest levels in a decade, threatening growth and dashing the hopes of an improved life for millions of poor blacks. 

 The rand has shed 30 percent of its value against the dollar since late May as speculators targeted the currency amid growing emerging market jitters. 

 The Johannesburg bourse has suffered a 42 percent collapse since April, taking stocks to levels not seen since the eve of South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994 when many feared a civil war. 

 The recent Russian financial crisis added to South Africa's woes last week, but Wednesday's session had seen stock and money markets begin to stabilise. 

 "That is a very bad report to have in these circumstances," another economist said in forecasting a tough day for domestic markets on Thursday. 

 The rand eased to around 6.23 (bid) to the dollar in overnight trading from 6.21 (bid) when the local market closed at 1400 GMT on Wednesday. 

 In its review, the IMF said South Africa's "uneven monetary policy" and buying of the rand on currency markets had exposed the economy to greater risk earlier this year. 

 "Directors expressed concern that, following an initial increase in interest rates, the authorities' intervention in the spot and forward exchange markets and the pursuit of an uneven monetary policy had exacerbated the pressures and may have risked converting a contagion problem into one that was more specific to South Africa," said the IMF report. 

 The IMF urged a comprehensive policy response to restore market confidence in the currency, including keeping a tight monetary policy, refraining from currency intervention, achieving government budget targets and accelerating previously announced reforms. 

 "If renewed pressures develop, the Reserve Bank (of South Africa) would need to tighten monetary policy again," the IMF report said. 

 It also warned that reducing interest rates too hastily would encourage inflation and risk a further speculative attack on the currency. 

 In hindsight, the central bank could have raised interest rates earlier to defend the currency, economists said, but they considered the IMF's criticism unfair. 

 "It's very easy to criticise the Reserve Bank, but you must remember at the time it was unclear that the contagion effect would go as far as it did," said John Reed of ABN-AMRO in Johannesburg. 

 There was no immediate comment from the central bank, but Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said earlier on Wednesday that global market turmoil prevented a quick rate reduction. 

 The central bank is facing growing domestic pressure to ease monetary policy as the country teeters on the edge of a recession. 

 Official rates have soared to 21.855 percent from 15 percent in April, threatening homeowners and businesses. 

 Stals said South Africa had the stamina to weather the storm buffeting world markets, but the immediate future was beyond official control. 

 "Return of stability to these markets will pave the way for lower rates in South Africa...For any individual country such as South Africa to break out of these shackles at this stage will be almost impossible," he said. 

 ((Johannesburg newsroom, 27 11 482 1003, newsroom@reuters.co.za)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: SAfrica's Stals says rand currently undervalued.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, July 30 (Reuters) - South African Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals said on Thursday that the heavy losses of the rand in an 11 week currency crisis had thrust the unit into oversold territory against the country's main trading partners. 

 "If you look at the average weighted value of the rand against the (trade weighted) basket of currencies...we have seen a depreciation of 20 percent. That is more than can be justified in terms of inflation differentials," he said. 

 Stals, speaking to journalists after addressing a South African Chamber of Business conference, said that the rand appeared to be stablising and that the central bank had been able to withdraw from intervention for much of July. 

 "We intervened in the first week of July but since then the market has become much more quiet and volumes have declined. On a net basis there was not that much intervention over the last three weeks," he said. 

South Africa's currency has slumped 20 percent since late May in the face of speculative attack, as widening concerns over emerging markets shook investor confidence worldwide and made the unit an easy target for foreign sellers. 

 Stals said that the rand now appeared cheap - but declined to predict when it might recover - if ever. 

 "The rand is certainly undervalued at the present level. But what is the right exchange rate and where will it be at the end of this year? (That) no one can really predict or forecast." 

 ((-Johannesburg newsroom, 27-11-482-1003 newsroom@reuters.co.za)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: FOCUS-SAfrica rand plunges as attack renewed.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, June 29 (Reuters) - South Africa's rand plunged on Monday as speculators renewed their month-long assault against the currency that has inflicted crushing losses against the dollar and pound. 

 The rand vaulted 6.00 against the dollar in a headlong slide to a fresh all-time low of 6.150. 

 This represents a 13 percent loss on Thursday morning's 5.420 against the dollar and 21 percent since May 22 when a widening emerging market crisis provoked the first blatant speculative attack. 

 Economists reckon the heavy decline in the rand's value is not justified by its macroeconomic fundamentals - which might be weak in some areas like the balance of payments and growth but are generally regarded as solid. 

 But this has cut little ice with hedge-fund sellers, who shrugged off reported intervention on behalf of the Reserve Bank of South Africa by the Federal Reserve and Bank of England late on Friday and on Monday were swift to take up cudgels again. 

 "This is a very unhappy situation. The rand's movement is not justified by fundamentals, but the global environment is not favourable," said economist Peter Worthington at JP Morgan. 

 Dealers reported unprecedented central bank aid from Britain and the United States on Friday afternoon, but this failed to halt the headlong slide. There has been no official comment on reports of a concerted round of intervention. 

 The Reserve Bank has limited options at its disposal to defend the rand. It is expected to lift official interest rates at its daily money market repo auction at 1000 GMT to back over 20 percent, from 18.31 percent on Friday. 

 But analysts fear a such a step would penalise the fragile economy and have little chance of scaring off speculators. 

 They were equally sceptical that official intervention could stem the tide running against the rand. 

 The country's gross official reserves stood at just 32.9 billion rand at the end of May - nowhere near enough to stave of market selling that time and again has demonstrated that it can master almost any amount of official support. 

 June reserves will be posted on Tuesday and a Reuters survey expected them to decline to around 31 billion rand. 

 No one was prepared to stick their neck out over how much the Bank's crucial uncovered position on its forward foreign exchange book would have changed over the month after it soared unexpectedly to $17.9 billion at end-May from $12.8 billion in April. 

 South Africa has now endured over a month of abuse at the hands of international currency speculators and JP Morgan's Worthington said it was extremely hard to judge when this would be exhausted. 

 But he predicted a sharp recovery in rand values when the selling stopped - mirroring the boost it gained when its last trail by foreign exchange dealer in 1996 ended. 

 Then, a collapse to 4.50 against the dollar from 3.60 on an attack sparked by fears over the health of President Nelson Mandela saw prices bounce back to 4.30 once the attack faded. ((Johannesburg newsroom, 27-11-482-1003 newsroom@reuters.co.za)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: S. Africa's Stals -2: Confusion Over Fed, BOE  Intervention
text:
Central bank officials contacted at the weekend were adamant the Fed and the BOE were using South African central bank funds - not their own - to support the rand. This is a crucial issue as it means speculators aren't suddenly pitted against the financial might of two of the world's biggest central banks as they seek to pummel the rand. 

 Stals said he didn't want to comment on the nature of Friday's intervention until he has discussed these events with the deputy governors and department heads who oversaw the Reserve Bank's actions. 

 The central bank chief was with visiting French President Jacques Chirac's entourage Friday evening as the dollar was bounding to its new record high at ZAR5.9650. 

 But Stals pointed out that the Reserve Bank holds part of its foreign currency reserves with other central banks and some commercial institutions abroad for intervention outside South African trading hours. 

 Given the latest attack on the rand occurred during New York trading, he said "little should be made" that intervention was funded from the bank's accounts at the Fed and the BOE. 

 However, central bank officials in South Africa conceded that there was a different twist to the intervention Friday, as dealers at the U.S. and U.K. central banks acted directly in addition to passing on the South African Reserve Bank's funds to commercial traders. 

 This aspect created the greatest furor in the currency market as it appeared the Fed and the BOE were prepared to put their own funds into supporting the rand.

title: Cenbank dlr/rand sales fail to impress-analysts.
text:
NEW YORK, June 26 (Reuters) - The South African rand on Friday plummeted to a record low, failing to grasp a lifeline extended in New York trade when central banks were seen helping Johannesburg bolster the battered rand. 

Currency dealers said both the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Bank of England sold the dollar against the rand on behalf of South Africa in mid-morning New York trading but later noted the efforts appeared fruitless. 

 Market players were surprised to see the U.S. central bank intervene and the rand briefly stabilised on the news. But it soon resumed its sharp decline and hit a low of 5.9605 rand to the dollar. 

 The Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the Bank of England and the Reserve Bank of South Africa all declined to comment when asked whether and why they had sold dollar/rand. 

 New York dealers said they saw the Federal Reserve sell at 5.74 and again at 5.71 while the Bank of England was seen selling at 5.6950. The sales caught the market by surprise and briefly stabilised the South African unit. 

Currency dealers quickly pronounced the intervention ineffective in stopping the rand's slide, possibly because markets realise South Africa has insufficient reserves to mount a longer-term rand defence. 

 "They (South African Reserve Bank) can't intervene and spend the world, because they don't have it. It's like the gun is empty and they've got to turn elsewhere for ammunition," said David Durrant, global currency strategist at consulting group I.D.E.A. 

 Dealers could not estimate the size of the intervention, though some said the central banks had been buying rand in chunks of $20 million. 

 South Africa "hasn't got much in the way of reserves, so we don't know exactly how much they did. While they moved it back up, obviously there was nothing behind it, so in that sense (the intervention) was a disaster," added Nick Douch, corporate risk advisor at Barclays Capital in London. 

 While Friday's move marked a dramatic shift for South Africa, which has previously preferred to intervene through commercial banks rather than foreign central banks, dealers said it was not enough. 

 "I think they probably asked the Fed and the Bank of England to help in order to make a statement, because anytime we see a big central bank in there it makes people nervous, but it doesn't seem to have worked," a New York dealer said. 

 With markets clearly ready to pummel the rand lower still, dealers and analysts agreed there was no way to predict where the decline may end or even slow. 

 "It is impossible to give levels here, we have been gapping all over the place," another dealer said. 

 The rand has come under increasing pressure since late May when speculators rounded on the currency after a worldwide crisis in emerging markets left it an easy target. The slump also came in spite of a firm increase in official interest rates Friday. 

 While South Africa weathered last summer's Asia crisis well, analysts were now bracing for more serious problems and agreed one way to help the rand more would be to express international concern. 

 "The only way you could get around this is if nations like the U.S. and the UK are genuinely worried and they would come out and say we are concerned with the way markets are treating these emerging markets and we are therefore intervening ourselves," Douch said. 

 But he and others said "there is very little chance that this would happen." 

 ((-NA Treasury Desk, 212-859-1639 )). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: S. Africa rand in freefall despite Fed report.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (Reuters) - The central banks of Britain and the United States rode to the rescue of South Africa's collapsing rand on Friday, dealers said, but the unprecedented support failed to stem the currency's slide. 

 Reports from New York dealers that the Federal Reserve and Bank of England had bought rand for dollars shocked analysts, who reckon that it was the first time that South Africa had enlisted U.S. and British help to boost its currency. 

 But the news failed to quell a savage speculative assault which has inflicted losses of over 8 percent against the dollar in just 24 hours. 

 Both the Federal Reserve and officials at the Reserve Bank of South Africa declined to confirm whether there had been a round of concerted intervention. The Bank of England also declined to comment. 

 The rand briefly hesitated when the reports were published - and then resumed its headlong slide. 

 Analysts fear that foreign sellers have 6.00 rand to the dollar in their sights and warned it was futile to damage the weak domestic economy by using interest rates to defend the currency against an all-out assault. 

 "If they fire the Fed and the BOE off and they still can't hold back speculators then God help everyone else," said John Clemmow, Africa analyst at Investec Securities in London. 

 The rand's losses rode roughshod over a firm increase in official interest rates earlier on Friday, which initially lent support to the country's battered bond and stock markets before fresh waves of rand selling put them back on the ropes. 

 Rand value against the dollar has been slashed from 5.080 since late May to a new low of 5.92 - or a fall of over 15 percent - as speculators rounded on the currency after a worldwide crisis in emerging markets left it an easy target. 

 Economists thought that the Bank had opted to let the market have its way, rather than waste hard-won foreign reserves in a futile bid to battle speculators. 

 The central bank intervened heavily to support the rand in May - employing 26 billion rand ($4.58 billion) to support the currency in the early stages of an emerging market assault. 

 Most of the intervention was taken through its forward foreign exchange book and the amount represents a significant share of its gross official reserves, which stood at 32.9 billion rand ($5.8 billion) at the end of May. 

 The Bank has since signalled it would revert to its well-worn strategy of "leaning against the wind" - only intervening to smooth the rand's descent. 

 But analysts wondered whether the Bank had decided to have another go at the speculators but lacked the fire-power needed. 

 "South African authorities don't have the means to intervene in the market, they don't have enough foreign exchange reserves," said economist Magan Mistry at Nedcor in Johannesburg. 

South Africa's alternative to intervention would be to allow interest rates to rise in the rand's defence, but a hike in official repo rates to 18.31 percent from 17.34 percent earlier on Friday failed to turn the tide. 

 Rates had soared to a 13-year high of almost 24 percent on Monday but had been allowed to relax over the week as a semblance of stability returned. 

 The run on the rand shattered any illusion that South Africa's economy was out of the woods. 

 Economists argue that the central bank should allow the rand to slip rather than chance a prolonged period of high interest rates, which would stifle essential growth and even topple the fragile economy into full-blown recession. 

 The stock market closed down but above session lows after a modest afternoon recovery pared losses to 61.7 points at 6,874.3. Bonds were spectators to the afternoon's gyrations, with most accounts happy to stick to the sidelines. 

 The benchmark R150s, due 2005-2007, closed at a yield of 14.75 percent. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: South African Rand Tumbles Despite Reported Joint  Intervention
text:
JOHANNESBURG, South Africa -(Dow Jones)- In what amounted to a new Black Friday for the South African currency market, the rand plunged about 6% against the dollar - its biggest single-day drop - and prompted the South African Reserve Bank to reportedly seek assistance from the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England. 

 The South African government, meanwhile, is facing growing pressure to engineer a new fiscal strategy to stabilize the beleaguered currency and to stave off a repeat of 1996, when the rand plunged 22% amid fears about the fledgling democracy's economic credentials. 

 The rand has tumbled more than 15% against the dollar this year, as the Asian economic crisis hobbled the fragile South African economy. Analysts said the rand was an easy target for speculators after the government eased its key repurchase, or repo, rate earlier in the week. Dwindling foreign reserve levels also left the currency vulnerable. 

 The country had sharply lifted interest rates recently to bolster its currency and keep investment within the country. In the past few days, though, it nudged the repo rate below its highest levels, which helped spark Friday's rand selling. 

 The reported intervention temporarily pushed the dollar down to around 5.7000 rand from just under 5.8000 rand. But the rand's strength quickly faltered, as the dollar's downward momentum was halted within half an hour of the first reports of Fed intervention. 

 The dollar then made a sharp recovery, soaring through 5.8000 rand and settling at 5.8950 rand in Johannesburg, up from 5.5875 Thursday. In New York trading, the dollar soared to a record high at 5.9655 rand from 5.5875 rand a day earlier. 

 None of the three three central banks would comment on their reported roles Friday in what appears to have been the first instance of concerted intervention for the South African currency. But traders in in London, New York and Johannesburg were adamant that the U.S. and British central banks had been in the market. 

 "I suspect that they (the Fed and the Bank of England) are doing it with South Africa's money, but the problem is South Africa doesn't have a lot of reserves," said Mark Chandler at Deutsche Bank Securities. 

 Chris Stals, head of the South African central bank, said he had no knowledge of whether the Federal Reserve and Bank of England bought rand for dollars on South Africa's behalf Friday. But he said it "isn't unusual" for other central banks to intervene on behalf of the South African Reserve Bank should currency weakness occur outside the Johannesburg market's hours. 

 The rand has been softening against the dollar on and off for several years, as South Africa continues to open up its once-insular economy to international competition following the dismantling of apartheid. 

 Traders had expected the rand to continue to fall against the dollar, but the declines in recent weeks have pushed the currency well past forecasts, and South Africa has largely depleted its reserves to defend the currency. 

 The weaker rand is of some benefit to the country. Although it makes imports more expensive for South African buyers, and raises fears of capital flight, the decline makes South African products less expensive for foreign buyers. Many economists in South Africa have felt the rand must depreciate further if South African exports are to compete on global markets. Meanwhile, many Asian and African currencies have fallen much more sharply than the rand. 

 Having depleted its scant holdings of foreign exchange heavily in May and early June to defend the rand - South Africa spent $6.60 billion to buy the rand in May before changing tack in mid-June by raising rates - most market participants believe the Reserve Bank really has no choice but to send rates sharply higher once again to defend the currency. 

 On Friday, the bank started to do just that. The repo rate rose to 18.31% at the daily tender from 17.35%, but the increase was well below market expectations. The repo rate reached a record 23.96% on Monday. The rate is the cost the South African Reserve Bank charges commercial banks to meet their daily borrowing requirements and is the most powerful mechanism for setting monetary policy. 

Central bank governor Rand said he believes monetary policy is still the most appropriate approach in dealing with the soft rand, and that it's "unlikely" the government will change its fiscal policy to address the weak currency. 

 But Peter Worthington, a currency analyst with J.P. Morgan in Johannesburg, said the government now needs to begin working on a revamp of its fiscal programs to lure offshore investors to South Africa. 

 Such a move would mirror the events of two years ago, when a sudden plunge by the rand in February 1996 brought a savage end to two years of stability and prodded the government to unveil its five-year Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy, subsequently known as GEAR. The GEAR policy outlined a government commitment to bringing down the budget deficit, creating new jobs by encouraging investment, removing exchange controls and privatizing some state assets. 

 While the rand has almost consistently weakened since February 1996, many economists credit the government's actions in unveiling the GEAR strategy with slowing the rate of its descent. 

 The first three months of 1998 brought substantial overseas investment into South Africa's equity and bond markets, a relatively modest decline in the value of the rand and a substantial improvement in the Reserve Bank's gold and foreign-exchange reserves. 

 But recent developments in Indonesia and Russia have soured investors' mood towards many emerging markets, precipitating renewed speculative attacks on the rand and heavy sales of South African bonds. 

 The depth of South Africa's social ills - crime, lack of housing and basic services and its young democracy - have marked it as an emerging economy. As such, there is still a high degree of currency risk. Investor confidence largely hinges upon the government's commitment to cutting its budget deficit and funding its massive social programs. 

 J.P. Morgan's Worthington believes the government needs to go further now to have the same impact it did in 1996. 

 "They need to issue a statement like GEAR and in it they should commit to accelerate privatization, take new steps to liberalize labor markets and do more to effectively tighten fiscal policy," he said. 

 But diagnosing and administering fresh fiscal medicine takes time, and Worthington said it is unlikely the government of President Nelson Mandela will announce any new action over the weekend or early next week.

title: SAfrica stocks to keep wary eye on rand and mkts.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, May 29 (Reuters) - South African stocks, emerging from their worst week since January, will keep a wary eye on a wobbly rand and volatile world markets next week, analysts said. 

 Despite a two percent rebound for Johannesburg shares on Friday, they said several risks were lurking in the wings for South African equities. 

 "In the short term I still think there is further weakness coming, particularly into next week," said Murray Winckler, an equity strategist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Johannesburg. 

 "We are now factoring in a higher risk premium into our markets and we believe in the next three to six months equity markets will reach new highs," he told Reuters. 

 Johannesburg's key All Share Index surrendered over six percent this week, including a five percent drop on Wednesday, as investors fled in the face of market turmoil at home and abroad - particularly in Russia and Asia. 

 The rand sank to record lows this week, forcing South Africa's Reserve Bank to hike interest rates and intervene in money markets to prop up the embattled currency. 

 But in equities, bargain hunters sparked a recovery on Friday, pushing the All Share Index up 2.2 percent by the close of trading. 

 Financial stocks, which bore the brunt of this week's selling, led the rebound with a 4.6 percent rally on Friday. 

 The sector suffered heavy losses this week amid fears that higher rates would narrow bank margins and trim profits. 

 South Africa's major banks held their prime lending rates in check, but analysts did not rule out a move next week to follow the central bank's nearly two percentage-point rate hike on Tuesday. 

 "There still seems to be a fairly even chance the banks could jack their prime rates up next week," Winckler said. 

 Equity traders will also keep an eye on next week's economic data, including gold and foreign exchange reserves data on Tuesday. 

 Local and offshore traders have speculated that the central bank's cash reserves have been drained by up to $2 billion dollars after its intervention in the foreign exchange market during the month. 

 However, some analysts said the reserves were likely to have fallen by only half that amount. 

 Richard Jesse, a director at Fleming Martin, said investors will have few corporate results to watch next week and will likely turn their attention to other world markets. 

 The only major earnings reports next week are conglomerate Tongaat-Hulett  on Monday and mining financial giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd  on Tuesday. 

 "You tend to find in June that results start to peter out. The market will probably occupy itself by looking closely at other world emerging markets and the U.S. market," Jesse said. 

 Firmer European stocks on Friday after Wall Street's higher close have eased market fears over emerging markets in Asia and Russia, which suffered heavy losses this week. 

 "We should have a less volatile week than the one we've just had. It has been a rather abnormal week," Jesse said. 

 Technical analysts said this week they expect South African stocks to stay in the grip of market bears for several months before the trend turns upward again. 

 They said a pullback was long overdue for a market that has soared 30 percent in the last four months. The All Share Index could work a range between 6,500 and 7,000 in the months ahead before resuming its climb, they added. 

 "The overall picture is more consolidation and pullbacks during the next four to five months and also more volatility," said technical analyst Victor Hugo. 

 "Generally negative sentiment until Asia and the emerging market picture stabilises," he added.

title: SAfrica cbk says not defending set dlr/rand level.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, April 1 (Reuters) - South Africa's Reserve Bank said on Wednesday it intervened in the market to smooth volatile conditions but said it was not defending any specific dollar/rand level. 

 "I think we have a concern if the rand were to move very sharply on the back of speculative trading, but are not protecting any particular level," said Bertus van Zyl, the Reserve Bank's general manager of international banking. 

 Earlier, traders said they believed the central bank had sold dollars for rand at 5.0450 in order to steady the rand's depreciation. 

 "There seems to be evidence that he (the Bank) is coming in around those levels (5.0450/dlr) but it is nothing aggressive. It's just leaning against the wind," said a senior foreign exchange dealer earlier. 

 When asked if the Bank was comfortable with a gradual easing in the rand's value against the dollar, Van Zyl answered "yes" and added that its involvement had been a precautionary measure to ensure an orderly market. 

 His comments followed those of Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals to a South African newspaper that he was "not unhappy" with the rand's recent slip to record lows against the dollar. 

 Van Zyl would not say to what extent the central bank had sold dollars or bought rand. 

 The rand slipped above the pyschologically important 5.00/dlr threshold on Monday after a spate of mixed economic data and in the face of a rampant dollar.

title: FOCUS-S.AFRICA RESERVES DIP IN BATTLE FOR RAND.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Dec 1 (Reuters) - South Africa's gold and foreign exchange reserves dipped slightly to 26.5 billion rand in November from October's 27.3 billion, but economists said on Monday this masked hefty intervention to defend the rand. 

South Africa's central bank said its use of foreign credit lines rose 1.1 billion rand to 9.9 billion by end November. 

 "Subtracting credit lines, the net reserves are worth around $3.4 billion, which is low by the standards of most countries. So the position of the reserves is still a concern," said UBS economist Costa Vayenas in London. 

 The data matched a Reuters consensus forecast carried out on November 28 which called for a fall to 26.5 billion rand. 

 It covered a month in which emerging markets around the world shuddered in a crisis of confidence as foreign investors ran for cover after Hong Kong stocks tumbled. 

 The rand plumbed fresh lows against the dollar and pound, and the stock and bond markets both suffered heavy losses in the fallout from the Asia epidemic. 

 But economists said that the rand could have fallen by more and speculated that it had been cushioned by heavy intevention by the central bank. 

 In the event it appeared that the intervention had been significant, but probably not unduly substantial against the background of a massive run on emerging market assets. 

 "It's not really a bad number given the context of the current environment in world financial markets," said Equisec economist Dawie Roodt in Johannesburg. 

 But this gave no grounds for complacency. 

 "The position is not good. Our reserves are far from sufficient -- they only cover around 10 weeks worth of imports -- but are at least better than last year," he said. 

 South African import cover is now running at 2-1/2 months' worth compared with less than a month this time last year. 

 Standard Bank economists calculated that this cover was eroded to only eight weeks in November's financial turmoil, but did not think the position was life-threatening. 

 "South Africa's sound economic fundamental situation should ensure that the current account deficit is more than offset by net capital inflows in 1998, resulting in renewed build-up of foreign reserves," it said in a note to clients.

title: SAfrica c.bank reserves seen hit by  intervention .
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 29 (Reuters) - South Africa's Reserve Bank is estimated to have spent up to $1.5 billion defending the rand against speculators in the last few days of market turmoil, which saw the currency forced to all-time lows, dealers said. 

 But market participants were less certain of the damage the central bank's strategy of measured dollar selling to smooth rand fluctuation had wrought on its foreign exchange reserves. 

 Total foreign exchange reserves stood at 21.1 billion rand at the end of September. The Reserve Bank will release October figures on Monday. 

 Dealers said the Bank was more active on Monday. 

 "At a rough guess they might have spent about $1.5 bln in two days but Tuesday might only have seen $100 million," said one Johannesburg forex chief who declined to be named. 

 "Tuesday was a more organised depreciation (in the rand) because even though it was moving up, it seemed to a lot of us to follow the bonds. There was a lot of two-way business so not much need for the Bank to support it," said another dealer. 

Foreign exchange investors were granted a respite on Wednesday as the rand stabilised around 4.81 to the dollar -- back from a 4.86/dollar record low plumbed on Tuesday. 

 "I think you might see (the Bank) bleeding off some excess dollars from the market, and there are a few stale longs from London, but the Bank's not going to aggressively come in and buy now," one dealer said. 

 Analysts said the rand's six cent decline, coupled with a more than 200 percent rise in the money market shortage since Saturday, could not help but pare reserves. 

 But opinions were mixed as to where in the Bank's balance sheet -- forward foreign exchange transactions, cash or utilisation of bank credit lines -- costs would be felt most. 

 "My own view is that they haven't dipped into the forward book. In other words, most of the liquidity given to the foreign exchange and money markets has come though spot reserves and possibly borrowed reserves," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Gordon Smith. 

 Another economist said: "They'll have done a combination (of spot and forward). They are trying to get their forward book down but if they needed to spend a lot then they would have made at least some use of that." 

 Others said the Bank might have stored additional dollars during the stability of early October, using them to soothe the rand's recent woes. 

 But economists said the Reserve Bank would generally be reluctant to deploy the forward book as it has been working hard to extract itself entirely from the expensive net oversold position it built over the first half of last year in defence of the rand, when the currency shed 20 percent against the dollar. 

 Economists and the International Monetary Fund have been urging the Bank to work faster on paring the forward books' oversold position -- revealed at $18 billion in August. 

 Some expressed concern that if the central bank drags its heels, it could invite the kind of speculative attacks recently seen in Thailand, which has paid a high price for undermining its apparently ample reserves with forward trades.

title: S. Africa Rand Falls On Fresh Dlr Surge, Local Bank Order

title: SAfrica Stals defends frx  intervention .
text:
PRETORIA, Aug 26 (Reuter) - South African Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday that he disagreed with the International Monetary Fund's stance against intervention by the central bank in the foreign exchange market. 

 "If we stop intervening in the markets today...interest rates will go up in South Africa substantially, but because we intervene in the market we try to keep interest rates at a reasonable level," he said. 

 In a statement released after a review of the South African economy the IMF argued that heavy purchases of the rand created confusion in the foreign exchange market and left the central bank open to the risk of big trading losses. 

 The rand last week hit a record low against the U.S. dollar of 4.7910 bid, before bouncing back in part because of determined buying by the bank. 

 Stals rejected any suggestion that South Africa's interest rates were too low. 

 "We do our best to try and keep some kind of average, middle policy that will satisfy both international capital flows and domestic economic needs," he said. 

 The IMF board had advised South African authorities to tighten financial policies rather than intervening in the market to protect the rand. 

 A few IMF directors even recommended that Pretoria increase interest rates should the rand face renewed heavy selling.

text:
Stals' announcement, which came at the Reserve Bank's annual general meeting, caught onlookers off guard. 

 Market participants had hoped that the central-bank chief would comment on monetary policy, but in the form of announcing a 1.0-percentage-point cut in the Bank rate to 16%, the first fall in four years. 

 In addition, the International Monetary Fund had only hours earlier declared in an annual review that the central bank should place less reliance on intervention and more on monetary policy to react to exchange-rate movements. 

 Stals said growth in the broad money supply and private-sector credit extension remain too high for an easing of monetary policy. He also rejected the IMF's suggested approach to influencing the rand, saying interest rates would rise immediately were the central bank to abandon the currency to market forces alone. 

 'We do our best to keep some kind of ... policy that will satisfy both international capital flows and domestic economic needs,' Stals told reporters. 'But the IMF has a very firm view on this: that we should not intervene in the forward foreign-exchange market or the foreign-exchange market. title: IMF urges forceful South African economic reforms.
text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuter) - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned South Africa on Monday its economy is vulnerable to the whims of foreign investors and urged it to press ahead with economic reforms for its own good and that of the region. 

 In a statement released after a recent review of the country's economy, the IMF board called on Pretoria to speed up its privatization program, cut trade tariffs, keep interest rates high and maintain a tight grip on government finances. 

 "Directors encouraged the authorities to forcefully implement their stabilization and adjustment strategy to help create a prosperous South Africa, which would not only benefit the people of South Africa but also the regional economy," the IMF said, summing up the board's discussion on July 11. 

 The IMF regularly reviews the economies of all its member nations. Subject to the agreement of the country, it then releases a summary of the talks. 

 The board welcomed South Africa's determination to reduce its budget deficit, but several directors cautioned that a recent wage agreement with civil servants might make that difficult. 

 The IMF also urged the country to take "bold initiatives" to increase job opportunities for unskilled workers through more flexible wage rates and stepped-up training. 

 But several IMF board directors cautioned the country against plans to levy a payroll tax to pay for increased training programs, arguing that might hinder job creation. 

 The board also took issue with South Africa's policy of intervening heavily in foreign exchange markets to prop up its currency, the rand. 

 It argued that heavy purchases of the rand created confusion in the foreign exchange market and left the central bank open to the risk of big trading losses. 

 The rand last week hit a record-low against the U.S. dollar before bouncing back, in part because of determined buying by South Africa's central bank. 

 Rather than intervening in the market to protect the rand, the IMF advised the South African authorities to tighten financial policies. 

 A few directors even recommended that Pretoria increase interest rates if the rand faces renewed heavy selling. 

 The board generally agreed that interest rates should not be cut, as the growth of money supply and credit remains well above target. 

 "Directors generally cautioned against an early reduction in the Bank rate," the IMF said.

title: IMF warns S. Africa against big  forex intervention .
text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuter) - The International Monetary Fund warned South Africa on Monday against heavy intervention in the foreign exchange market to shore up its currency and instead urged it to carry out tough economic reforms. 

 In a statement released after a review of the country's economy, the IMF board argued that heavy purchases of the rand created confusion in the foreign exchange market and left the central bank open to the risk of big trading losses. 

 "(The board) cautioned against large-scale intervention in foreign exchange markets," the IMF said, summarizing a discussion that took place on July 11. 

 The rand last week hit a record-low against the U.S. dollar, before bouncing back, in part because of determined buying by South Africa's central bank. 

 The currency was under pressure for most of 1996, in what the IMF described as a "stark change in investor sentiment" about South Africa's future. To keep the rand from falling further, the country's central bank intervened heavily in the currency market, building large forward position. 

 The IMF said its board of directors was concerned about the central bank's big net open forward position and stressed the importance of reducing it "on a sustainable basis." 

 "Further upward pressures (on the rand) should be used to reduce (the forward position)," the IMF said. "Substantial downward pressures on the rand should be resisted through a tightening of financial policies," it added. 

 A few directors even advised Pretoria to increase interest rates if the rand faced renewed heavy selling. 

 The board generally agreed that interest rates should not be cut, as the growth of money supply and credit remains well above target. 

 "Directors generally cautioned against an early reduction in the Bank rate," the IMF said. 

 The board urged South Africa to press ahead with tough economic reforms, saying that would help not only the country but the region as well. 

 It specifically called on Pretoria to speed up its privatization program and to use the money to pay down its debt. It also urged wide-ranging cuts in trade tariffs. 

 The board welcomed the country's determination to reduce its budget deficit, but several directors fretted that a recent wage agreement with civil servants might make that difficult. 

 It also called on the country to take "bold initiatives" to increase job opportunities for unskilled workers through more flexible wage rates and stepped-up training. 

 Several directors though cautioned the country against plans to levy a payroll tax to pay for increased training programs, arguing that might hinder job creation. 

 "Directors encouraged the authorities to forcefully implement their stabilization and adjustment strategy to help create a prosperous South Africa, which would not only benefit the people of South Africa but also the regional economy," the IMF said, summing up the board's discussion.

title: S.African rand ends off worst after new fall.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Aug 1 (Reuter) - South Africa's embattled rand plunged again on Thursday, hitting new lows against the British pound and the German mark before finishing off worst levels on perceptions the sell-off may have been overdone. 

 In early trade, it hit 4.53 against the dollar -- a level last seen in the eye of the rand storm three months ago -- but recovered to 4.49 soon after the 1400 GMT official close. 

 A weaker dollar helped the rand in late trade, dealers said. 

 The rand set an all-time low against sterling of 7.0455 rand while against the mark it slid to 3.0816 rand. 

 This week's renewed rand slide, which economists believe is unwarranted in terms of South Africa's economic fundamentals, has been blamed on market sentiment. 

 Technical charts, predicting future price moves from past developments, also paint a gloomy picture. 

 "There is still a demand for dollars both from locally and offshore because of the sentiment at the moment," said Willie Potgieter, director of foreign exchange at Standard Bank. 

 Traders say sentiment is being driven by factors including: 

 - labour opposition to government's macro-economic strategy. 

 - recurring rumours that Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals plans to resign despite his denials, repeated again this week. 

 - a recent batch of poor data on money supply, trade balance and inflation. 

 - and slow progress on privatisation and the removal of exchange controls. 

 President Nelson Mandela echoed economists' views that there was no direct reason for the rand's fall and also moved to quell the rumours about Stals, saying that he thought Stals was "the best man for the job". 

 "I am also convinced from what he has told me that he is prepared to serve for as long as we want him. I have no reason to doubt his sincerity in giving me that statement," Mandela told reporters in Pretoria on Thursday. 

 Stals, appointed in the apartheid era, is seen as a strong supporter of cautious monetary policy designed to keep inflation in check. 

 Edward Osborn, consultant to stockbroker Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd, felt the currency's weakness stemmed from a general lack of confidence in South Africa which had not been improved by government's unveiling of its macro-economic strategy in June. 

 "As we are being seen abroad, this is not a dynamic economy at the moment. It's pretty flat and full of political problems," he said. 

 The central bank has little in its power to stem the exodus from the rand, having intervened several times in the past five months only to see its holding of gold and foreign exchange reserves dwindle to about one month's import cover. 

 Board of Executors economic consultant Rob Lee said the bank's limited ability to intervene in favour of the rand meant South Africa was now dependent on net inflows of capital on a virtually daily basis.

title: S.African rand moves into uncharted territory.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Aug 1 (Reuter) - South Africa's embattled rand continued its plunge on Thursday, hitting new lows against the British pound and the German mark. 

 In early trade, the rand hit 4.53 against the dollar -- a level last seen in the eye of the rand storm three months ago. 

 The all-time low against sterling was 7.0455 rand while against the mark it slid to 3.0816 rand. 

 The renewed rand slide, which economists believe is unwarranted in terms of South Africa's economic fundamentals, has been blamed on currency traders. 

 Technical charts, predicting future price moves from past developments, also paint a gloomy picture. 

 "There is still a demand for dollars both from locally and offshore because of the sentiment at the moment," said Willie Potgieter, director of foreign exchange at Standard Bank. 

 Traders say sentiment is being driven by factors including: 

 - labour opposition to government's macro-economic strategy; 

 - recurring rumours that Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals plans to resign despite his denials, repeated again this week; 

 - a recent batch of poor data on money supply, trade balance and inflation; 

 - and slow progress on privatisation and the removal of exchange controls. 

 President Nelson Mandela echoed economists' views that there was no direct reason for the rand's fall and also moved to quell the rumours about Stals, saying that he thought Stals was "the best man for the job". 

 "I am also convinced from what he (Stals) has told me that he is prepared to serve for as long as we want him. I have no reason to doubt his sincerity in giving me that statement," Mandela told reporters in Pretoria on Thursday. 

 Stals, appointed in the apartheid era, is seen as a strong supporter of cautious monetary policy designed to keep inflation in check. 

 Edward Osborn, consultant to stockbroker Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd, felt the currency's weakness stemmed from a general lack of confidence in South Africa which had not been improved by government's unveiling of its macro-economic strategy in June. 

 "As we are being seen abroad, this is not a dynamic economy at the moment. It's pretty flat and full of political problems," he said. 

 The central bank has little in its power to stem the exodus from the rand, having intervened several times in the past five months only to see its holding of gold and foreign exchange reserves dwindle to about one month's import cover.

title: Rand's fall is early warning to cool euphoria.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Feb 21 (Reuter) - The collapse of the rand has raised fears of a repeat of 1995's Mexican financial crisis, but economists said on Wednesday there were important differences which should prevent South African markets spiralling out of control. 

 Dave Mohr, chief economist at assurer Old Mutual, said the rand fall was an early warning to government and investors, who may have been gripped by unsustainable euphoria recently. 

 "Maybe we were getting onto a Mexican wave, and we've had at least an early warning from the markets that everything is not hunky-dory with economic policy," he said. "But I don't think it's as serious as Mexico." 

 The rand has fallen nearly 10 percent and bonds 12 percent since last Thursday, hit by unfounded rumours about President Nelson Mandela's health and talk of an imminent easing in foreign exchange controls. 

 The plunge of the Mexican peso, which led to sharp falls in share and bond prices in emerging markets, was exacerbated by fruitless central bank intervention. 

 In contrast South Africa's central Reserve Bank appeared to be adopting a relatively hands-off approach, despite sporadic intervention to smoothe market fluctuations, analysts said. 

South Africa's pummelling at the hands of the international capital markets was the latest example of how vulnerable developing economies can be to the sentiments of foreign investors, analysts said 

 "It looks like a bit of a confidence crisis which can turn around as quickly as it developed," said Tony Twine of Econometrix. But he cautioned that "anything is possible". 

 Analysts said a growing consensus among foreigners that the rand was overvalued had fuelled the currency's slide. 

 The same foreign investors had been largely responsible for the strength of the rand by pouring money into local bonds and stocks during 1995, noted Edward Osborn, consultant at Edey, Rogers & Co. 

 "They are getting their money out and pulling the rand down all the time," he said. 

 Another analyst said some foreign investors were running scared. "The guys got badly burnt in Mexico...Some foreigners lost 30 or 40 percent of their money overnight...everyone's just panicking because we don't have a lot of reserves," he said. 

 South Africa's reserves stood at 15.5 billion ($3.9 billion) in January -- levels which the Bank has said it would be attempting to bolster before exchange controls were relaxed any further. The country also has standby reserves at the International Monetary Fund. 

 Economists said the Reserve Bank's avowed policy of being present only to "soothe" the market's fluctuations would ensure the unit settled at a level which was more sustainable. 

 "The reserves are certainly totally inadequate to mount any sort of defence...It's spitting into the wind," said Osborn.

title: Rand crashes in Europe, hits all time low.
text:
LONDON, Feb 16 (Reuter) - The South African rand was sold in Europe, with continued liquidation forcing it down to a new all time low versus the dollar. 

 Funds out of Europe and some in the U.S. were looking for reasons to sell and rumours that exchange controls were about to be lifted, although denied, hit the currency. 

 At 1220 GMT the rand was quoted at 3.80/81 per dollar -- a massive spread compared with the usual 20 or 25 ticks -- more than four percent down from Thursday's high. The old all time low of 3.7155 was set on July 26, 1994. 

 "These are the excuses people are using but the bottom line is that it's been a great yield play," said one trader. 

 "The whole market was all round the same way playing the yield, and bang," he said. "Everyone was short dollars, there was only one way it could go." 

 Traders said because the rand had been steady for so long a major imbalance had built up with exporters hedging their dollar receipts forward to take advantage of the yield while the importers were happy to hold off and do nothing. 

 "The market appears to have got itself heavily oversold having been taking the yield on the stable rand ever since the abolition of the financial rand," said Macer Gifford, exotic currency specialist at Standard Chartered in London. 

 South African Finance Minister Chris Liebenberg denied a relaxation of exchange controls was imminent and the finance ministry said earlier that there had been no change in the plan to phase the lifting of restrictions. 

 Dealers said it is now up to the Reserve Bank of South Africa to intervene and restore some order to the market and there has been talk of covert central bank buying on the open market this morning. 

 In a research paper published earlier this week UBS said the rand was seven to 10 percent overvalued versus the dollar. 

 "According to our purchasing power parity estimates, the rand is now some 7-10 percent overvalued against the U.S. dollar," the paper said. 

 "With the current account balance set to worsen the rand's current trading range can only be sustained if measures are adopted to reduce overheating pressures in the economy and to cut the growing current account deficit," it said.

title: S.Africa's Stals opposes undue rand gain right now.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Feb 20 (Reuter) - South Africa's Reserve (central) Bank will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to prevent an undue appreciation of the rand at this stage, the Bank's governor Chris Stals said. 

 "In the current situation and pending certain exchange control relaxations, the Reserve Bank will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market in order to prevent an undue appreciation of the rand at this stage," he said in a statement announcing a tightening of monetary policy. 

 Within the framework of existing exchange controls on capital outflows, any excessive inflow of foreign capital could, at least before exchange controls are relaxed, exert pressures for an appreciation of the exchange rate, he said. 

 To relieve these, the Bank must intervene regularly in the market to absorb the surplus foreign exchange and to prevent a rand appreciation which would, at this stage, contribute further to the erosion of South Africa's competitive position in international markets. 

 It was an illusion to believe South Africa could be made more competitive merely by devaluing the currency, he said. 

Intervention to prevent any undue rand appreciation did however create prime liquidity and, if not counteracted or sterilised, added to the ability of banking institutions to provide more credit to their clients, he said. 

 Over the past seven months, the Reserve Bank's net foreign reserves rose 6.8 billion rand, resulting in a similar amount of liquidity being created by the central bank. 

 This conflict of objectives, to raise foreign reserves and prevent an undue rand appreciation on the one hand, and on the other to keep money supply under control, required the use of more than just discount rate as a monetary policy instrument. 

 Hence the announced tightening of banks' minimum reserve requirements as part of a new package to tighten monetary policy, including a rise in discount rate to 14 from 13 percent. 

 He said there was a "dire" need for the central bank to raise its foreign reserves to a more acceptable level. Their present value at 11.3 billion rand was barely enough to cover six weeks' imports and should be raised to a level of at least three months' imports, he said. 

 The bank therefore used every opportunity to obtain surplus foreign currencies from the foreign exchange market to supplement its reserves, he added.

Both consumer spending and business fixed investment is bound to be hampered far beyond the end of a lockdown, the analyst says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

Futures tied to the S&P 500 are down 0.1%, suggesting the benchmark index will open slightly lower. "Investors are just pausing for a breather after yesterday's excitement about the potential development of a vaccine," Gimber says. A successful vaccine would clear the way for a faster recovery in economic growth, he adds, but "clearly there's a long way to go before that would come into practice." Gimber doesn't expect major news from Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell 's congressional testimony. "We learned quite a lot about his position last week," he says. (joe.wallace@wsj.com)

Investors have "felt a wave of relief" that EU leaders are "finally realizing the need for fiscal stimulus" rather than "simply more monetary debt obligation," he says. EUR/USD rises 0.3% to 1.0954 after reaching a two-week high of 1.0977 earlier, according to FactSet. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0756 ET - May's ZEW index rose for the second consecutive month amid the coronavirus pandemic for both the eurozone and Germany, driven by a noticeable improvement in expectations, Oxford Economics' Katharina Koenz says. "Financial markets' expectations rose on the back of ample fiscal easing, historic monetary stimulus by all major central banks and the hope that the worst of the pandemic is behind us as countries have started to ease restrictions on economic activity," the economist says. Still, the safe-haven status of Danish government bonds could be an incentive to buy them, he says. At Wednesday's Danish auction of November 2022- and November 2029-dated government bonds, Nordea prefers the longer-dated bond. title: UPDATE 1- South Africa 's  central bank  will  intervene  if  fx  orderly function threatened
text:
(Adds details, quotes)

JOHANNESBURG, Oct 2 (Reuters) - South Africa's central bank will only intervene to protect the currency if "excess volatility or abrupt and disorderly adjustments" threaten the orderly functioning of the market, the deputy governor said on Tuesday.

"Policy flexibility requires that foreign exchange intervention continues to be part of the monetary policy toolkit to support economic and financial stability," Deputy Governor Daniel Mminele said in a speech delivered in New York that was posted on the bank's website.

The Reserve Bank two weeks ago resisted political pressure and kept benchmark rates unchanged at 6.5 percent.

The Reserve Bank's (SARB) September meeting was closely watched after its emerging market peers Turkey and Russia raised their main lending rates to keep in check inflation driven higher by weakening currencies.

The rand has fallen close to 20 percent against the dollar this year while yields on bonds have also spiked.

The 4-3 decision to keep rates pat rather than hike also exposed tensions between policymakers and the ruling party which has previously argued for a closer alignment of fiscal and monetary policy.

The governing African National Congress (ANC) released and then retracted a statement calling on the bank to do more to support the economy and cash-strapped consumers. The ANC voted in December to change the bank's ownership from private to public.

"The SARB has allowed the exchange rate to act as a shock absorber and adjustment mechanism," Mminele said.

"This does not mean that we are totally indifferent to exchange rate movements. It also does not mean that there cannot be circumstances where the cost of not intervening to dampen excess volatility or abrupt and disorderly adjustments, could be higher than that of intervening."

(Reporting by Mfuneko Toyana, editing by Ed Osmond)
