Government debt also weakened, pushing the yield on the benchmark three-year bond up 6 basis points to 6.08 percent, pulling back further from a record low of 5.97 percent hit last week.

The longer-dated 2026 paper fell more heavily, with its yield rising nearly 10 basis points to 8.095 percent.

The rand, one of the most heavily traded and freely floating of emerging market currencies, was at 8.5015 at 1505 GMT, its third straight session on the back foot as the euro, the currency of South Africa's biggest trading partner, fell against the dollar.

Doubts over whether a European summit later this week will make any headway in resolving the bloc's debt crisis weighed on the single currency, and by extension emerging market assets.

"The rand is reacting in a normal way to the euro falling," said Murat Toprak, a regional currency strategist at HSBC.

"But underperformance of the rand is more than usual, because when you look at the other currencies within the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, the magnitude of the weakness is not that big."

Turkey's lira, for instance, was only 0.5 percent weaker after the central bank intervened by tightening liquidity after the currency fell on concerns about escalating political tension with Syria after the shooting down of a Turkish war plane.

A wider South African current account deficit revealed last week as a result of a slowdown in exports are also weighing on the rand.

The Reserve Bank publishes its business cycle indicator for April on Tuesday and producer price, money supply and May trade figures are due later in the week - all of them likely to be closely watched for signs of the health of Africa's biggest economy.

JOHANNESBURG, May 31 (Reuters) - South Africa's rand hit a fresh six month low against the dollar early on Thursday before recouping some of its losses but could resume a slide towards 8.6 as Europe's debt woes drive investors away from emerging market assets to perceived safer havens.

The local unit fell to 8.58 to the greenback, its weakest since late November, before clawing back some ground to 8.5330 by 0650 GMT.

"There is a possibility of some pull-back as exporters step in this morning but the real core of the matter still remains this massive uncertainty in Europe and risk-off associated with that," said market analyst Quinten Bertenshaw of ETM.

" The core focus for most people is to stay long dollars so I would suggest that any dips back towards 8.40 will bring back the buyers with an eventual target of 8.60," he added.

Governor Gill Marcus again ruled out any central bank intervention to support the rand late on Wednesday, saying using foreign exchange reserves to do this would not be good use of the money.

"If you take that path, you've got to have very deep pockets. We don't think it is good use of our money. It is very expensive," Marcus told a forum.

On Thursday, traders said the market would only pay passing attention to domestic producer inflation and trade data for April, which should largely confirm price pressures are fairly benign, while problems in Europe, a key trading partner for South Africa, continue to constrain local exports.

Emerging markets are seeing greater exchange rate volatility as near-zero interest rates in developed economies lead investors to seek yields in riskier but higher yielding assets.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt Buoyed As Dollar Weakens
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and debt mostly had a strong run Wednesday as talk of more quantitative easing pushed the dollar weaker.

The day was full of big headlines that moved markets during various continental trading hours. Standard & Poor's change of India's sovereign outlook to negative sharply weakened the Indian rupee during the day. Then, the European Commission opened the doors for Hungary to begin negotiations with the European Union and International Monetary Fund, leading to the forint hitting a nine-week high against the euro.

During the New York afternoon, the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee indicated that the central bank could pump more liquidity into the system. This turned into a dollar negative, and led to further appreciation of emerging-market currencies.

The dollar's weakness reverses days of ambivalent trading that was characterized by modest volumes and investors' reluctance to make any strong bets.

On Wednesday, the Hungarian forint was the leader on the board, as it appreciated nearly 2% against both the dollar and the euro. Investors and analysts cautioned against reading too much into the Hungarian government's actions, calling it the first step in a long process of securing backup support for Hungary's debt burden.

Still, investors and hedge funds rushed to cover their shorts on the currency, leading to strong demand and a rapid firming up of the currency. Risk premiums on Hungary's sovereign debt tightened by more than 48 basis points to 552 basis points over comparable Treasury yields.

In the New York afternoon, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke reiterated that the central bank is "entirely prepared" to embark on actions and programs to support the U.S. economy. Emerging-market currencies surged as another round of quantitative easing would trigger a fresh round of buying of these higher-yielding assets by investors.

The dollar was at ZAR7.7484 against the South African rand, down 0.63% on the day, and back to levels at the start of this month.

Similarly, the dollar was at TRL1.7692 against the Turkish lira, down 0.65% on the day, and back to levels at the start of March.

Brazil remained the outlier, with the dollar strengthening against the real after interventions by the central government. The dollar was trading at BRL1.8819, a tad stronger than its Tuesday close of BRL1.8793.

Also, if the Fed adopts another round of quantitative easing, then more central banks may follow Brazil's lead in making moves to curb local currency strength. Already, most of these countries blame the rounds of easing in the developed world for their appreciating currencies and surges in speculative capital flows to their local markets. Brazil, the most aggressive of all, has initiated a range of taxes and interventions to depreciate its currency. Other central banks, from South Korea to Peru, are constantly in the market, intervening to lower the volatility of their currencies. South Africa is calling for coordinated capital control, and its finance minister said this topic dominated chats at the recent IMF meetings.

Meanwhile, emerging-market sovereign debt was stronger, with risk premiums five basis points tighter to 351 basis points over comparable Treasury yields. Risk premiums on Argentina's debt narrowed more than 27 basis points to 977 basis points, as the sovereign debt, which is vulnerable to strong swings in investor sentiment, benefited from the broad market sentiment.

title: S.Africa's ANC mulls wider  central bank  mandate - paper
text:
* ANC contemplates constitutional changes - report

* Reserve bank mandate "narrow," may require review

* Reserve Bank should weaken rand exchange rate

JOHANNESBURG, March 4 (Reuters) - The ruling African National Congress (ANC) is mulling reforms to South Africa's constitution which would include changing the central bank's powers and price stability mandate, a local paper reported on Sunday.

City Press newspaper quoted the ANC as saying elements of the constitution that may require review included the "narrow mandate of the Reserve Bank or the relationship between and powers of the different spheres of government".

The government set the bank's monetary policy goal as containing inflation, which the bank does with a flexible inflation targeting strategy, aiming for a 3 to 6 percent inflation rate since 2000.

The South African Reserve Bank is perceived to be independent of government even as it regularly consults with the finance ministry. Its ultimate accountability is to parliament.

Inflation breached the bank's target in November and stood at 6.3 percent in January partly on the rising cost of imports into South Africa.

The Reserve Bank sees inflation returning back within the band only in the first quarter of 2013.

A strong rand shields the country from some inflation pressure, however unions bemoan the exchange rate, urging the Reserve Bank to intervene to weaken the currency and make South Africa's exports more competitive.

NOT ENOUGH FIREPOWER

Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus has continually said the bank does not target a level of the rand and buys foreign currency on the market to build up its reserves. The bank previously had an exchange-rate targeting mandate.

Its reserves, at about $49 billion in January, would not provide the bank with enough firepower to intervene in markets regularly.

The paper said some members of the ANC were calling for the inflation targeting strategy to be scrapped.

A senior official at the department of trade and industry criticised the Reserve Bank for not taking action against the "overvalued" rand, saying other central bank's manage their exchange rates while South Africa was following an old inflation targeting view.

"This is a wrong policy, you have to intervene to stabilise the currency when it becomes too strong," Lionel October, director-general at the department, said.

The rand closed weaker at 7.54 against the dollar on Friday but is seen strengthening in the short term as a long term liquidity injection from the European Central Bank funds carry trades.

The ANC, which holds a policy-setting conference in June, will release draft policy discussion documents to its branches on Monday. Proposals in the discussion papers would have to be adopted at another conference in December to shape government policy.

title: DJ UPDATE: Emerging Economies May See Repeat Of Inflationary Cycle
text:
-- LTRO expected to spur investors to buy EM assets

-- Some EM central banks, however, resist currency appreciation

-- Rising oil and commodity prices bring back inflation fears

(Updates to add details throughout) 


 
   By Prabha Natarajan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--The global economy is seeing echoes of 2009 and 2010, where easy monetary policy from advanced countries created a vicious cycle in which emerging markets attracted short-term money inflows from yield-seeking investors that in turn led to currency interventions and inflationary forces.

This risk, some say, is that this cycle--in which some see the makings of a competitive depreciation "currency war"--will exacerbate the problem of imported inflation and eventually force emerging market central banks to hike interest rates. That in turn could give rise to a "hard landing" slowdown in growth for both emerging markets and the world as a whole.

On Wednesday, the European Central Bank loaned EUR529.30 billion to 800 European banks. This boost in liquidity is expected to send a fresh influx of buyers into emerging market currencies, which had already recovered more than half of their 2011 losses within the first six weeks of this year, largely in response to a similar ECB action in December.

To add to their concerns, the resumption of a rapid surge in oil and commodity prices adds to the inflation challenges facing developing economies and limits their room for maneuver.

To be sure, emerging market countries' currencies and economies benefit from the incoming foreign capital, but many of them struggle to keep pace with the rapid pace of change in currency valuation, which make life harder for their key export industries. Back in 2009 and 2010, rapid exchange rate appreciation led policymakers to impose capital controls and intervene to weaken their currencies, both of which can scare off needed long-term investors.

Many economists are sympathetic to these countries' positions--a paper released Wednesday by the traditionally hands-off International Monetary Fund even advocated "temporary" intervention as a tool for containing volatility. But it's also widely recognized that central banks run can stoke inflation if they keep their currencies too weak, mostly because it makes imports more expensive than they would otherwise be. Eventually that can prompt a countervailing response with interest rates, which in turn could stall growth in the emerging market world. This is pretty much how the cycle played out in 2010.

"There's a sense of deja vu of last year, when [such easing in developed markets] triggered emerging market economies to start currency wars," said Alessio de Longis, portfolio manager of Oppenheimer Currency Opportunities Fund.

The situation turns particularly volatile when rising oil and commodity prices are thrown into the mix, as they are now. Net oil importing countries get hit with an immediate inflation threat and although energy producer countries such as Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Russia, Colombia and Malaysia benefit from higher export receipts, the currency appreciation challenge is even bigger in these countries.

While emerging market central banks can justify intervening against speculative moves in the currency, it's harder to explain countering capital flows that finance its growth. "Central banks have to strike a fine balance resisting currency appreciation but not turning away investors," de Longis said.

Capital flows into emerging economies are an "intense challenge," especially when these countries are easing rates, said Brazilian Central Bank President Alexandre Tombini, whose country has been a magnet for foreign money inflows, at a presentation on Wednesday. Already this year, the Brazilian central bank has initiated dollar purchases to weaken the real and on Thursday the government expanded the coverage of a tax on foreign currency loans to cover those of three-year periods from the previous two year limit. Tombini also reiterated his belief that the central bank can get its benchmark Selic rate down to single digits, from its current level of 10.5%, which should make the real less attractive.

The dollar is trading at BRL1.7176, currently, and many analysts see little upside potential to the currency.

Other central banks have joined the fray. Colombia has begun interventions and South Africa is buying dollars again. Others with strengthening currencies, such as Mexico and Chile, are likely for now to stick with monetary easing rather than direct intervention.

Indeed, until now, it was thought that many central banks--including the all important People's Bank of China--would be able to recover the growth lost last year by continuing to ease monetary conditions. But if inflation rears up again, not all central banks will be able to cut rates to boost domestic growth, said Guillaume Tresca, emerging market strategist at Credit Agricole .

"Inflation has accelerated in Central Europe, and higher oil and commodity prices could lead only to higher prices," he said.

Tresca expects emerging market currencies to face a correction in the coming weeks as the focus shifts to oil prices and return of inflation concerns. While there may be some currencies that do well, emerging Europe outside of Russia is expected to retreat, he said.

--By Prabha Natarajan, Dow Jones Newswires ; 212-416-2468; prabha.natarajan@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Flight From Risk Thrashes Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt
text:
-Global economic anxieties pummel emerging-market assets

-Host of central banks suspected of intervening as their currencies tumble

-South Africa, the Czech Republic hold policy rates steady


 
   Cynthia Lin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market assets fell under severe pressure Thursday as fears about the euro-zone credit crisis and global economic slowdown hit a boiling point despite the Federal Reserve's latest stimulus plan.

U.S. central bankers confirmed market expectations Wednesday, announcing that it will implement what most market participants call "Operation Twist," by buying longer-dated Treasurys and selling shorter-dated ones. The central bank's decision did little to allay mounting fears about the sputtering global economy, sparking an exodus out of risky assets and into the refuge of U.S. government debt.

As Treasury yields plummeted, the risk premium investors demand to hold what they perceive as riskier emerging-market debt increased. This spread as reflected on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, was 32 basis points wider to 449 basis points above Treasurys. In price terms, the index lost 1.49%. The Latin America regional sub-index lost 1.69% in price as its spread blew out 34 basis points to 5.14% over Treasurys.

Emerging-market currencies also took a beating across the board as the U.S. dollar soared, led by notable declines in the Mexican peso, Chilean peso and Korean won.

A slew central banks in Asia--including Korea, Taiwan and Thailand--were suspected to have intervened in the foreign exchange markets to lend support to their currencies. The Korean won was a notable underperformer in its region, weakening to KRW1,181.1 a dollar from KRW1,148.6--now the weakest since last September, according to CQG.

In Brazil, the country's central bank announced midday and quickly implemented an auction of $2.7 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts to rein in the depreciating real. The battered Brazilian currency opened at 1.92 reais to the dollar, weakening sharply to BRL1.94 at one point. On the Embig, Brazil's risk premium increased 29 basis points to 285 basis points, losing 0.97% in price.

Such efforts come in stark contrast to moves these central banks conducted just months ago, when many complained that their currencies were strengthening too quickly and hurting exporters at home. Earlier in the year, these assets showed impressive resilience even when the situation in advanced nations began to crumble. But the rout since the start of September shows that these regions are still inextricably linked to the developed world.

"The emerging-market space is interesting because it held and held and held," said Michael Mata, portfolio manager at ING's global bond fund, "but, in the end, there's no way to decouple from 50% of global GDP." Mata's team believes there's still more room from emerging-market currencies to fall as these nations' policymakers cut rates and reduce the interest-rate differential that made their currencies so appealing.

These days, inflation and other issues that come with red-hot economic growth is taking a back seat, with fears of a double-dip recession and the intensifying euro-zone credit crisis dominating investors' fears. The latest economic reports Thursday show the euro zone's composite purchase manufacturing index falling into the sub-50 contraction territory for the first time since 2009, while China's PMI sank deeper in the contraction range to 49.4 from 49.9.

South Africa's central bank decided to keep its policy rate at 5.5%, caught in a dilemma of slowing growth and rising inflation. The South African rand weakened to ZAR8.2963 a dollar from ZAR8.2530, which Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus acknowledged is putting the country's goal of keeping inflation under 6% at risk.

Monetary authorities of the Czech Republic also convened Thursday and decided to keep rates steady a record-low 0.75%. Central and Eastern European currencies have been rattled this month give their ties to the neighboring euro zone.

By Cynthia Lin; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-S.Africa's Davies says rand overvalued
text:

JOHANNESBURG, June 6 (Reuters) - South Africa's rand currency is overvalued and the government is currently discussing what to do about it, the country's trade minister said on Monday.

"Do we have a desirable currency? We don't," Rob Davies said at a media briefing in suburban Johannesburg.

"The rand is overvalued. What can we do about it? That is a difficult question... The discussion about what are going to do about it is ongoing."

The rand <ZAR=D3> has gained about 14 percent against the dollar in the last 12 months, drawing concern from both manufacturers and unions.

A stronger rand is a negative for exporters, as it eats into profits when revenues from abroad are brought home.

The rand has helped to contain inflation, which has been inside the central bank's 3 to 6 percent target band since February 2010.

Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan said last month South Africa was fortunate to have a stronger rand and the goverment would not intervene to weaken the currency. [ID:nLDE74306D]

South Africa last year spent over 15 billion rand ($2.24 billion) helping the Reserve Bank to accumulate reserves to limit rand gains.

The bank has said it does not target a level for the exchange rate but will continue to build reserves "as and when" appropriate.

South Africa last year rejected the idea of taxing capital inflows such as those implemented by Brazil and other emerging markets.

Manufacturers would rather see the rand at about 8.50 to the dollar.

title: UPDATE 2-Gordhan says S.Africa not planning rand  intervention
text:
* Rand gains have helped with inflation

* Govt still concerned about capital inflows

* Trade Minister says rand overvalued

(Adds details, background)

CAPE TOWN, May 4 (Reuters) - South Africa's government is not planning to intervene to weaken the rand currency that has helped to cushion the impact of higher oil and food prices, Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan said on Wednesday.

The government's rand policy is a touchy issue between the ruling African National Congress and its leftist allies who would rather see the currency weakened and Gordhan's comments could add to ongoing tensions in the alliance over policy.

The rand has gained more than 30 percent against the dollar since the beginning of 2009. It hit its strongest levels in more than three years this week and was last trading at 6.64.

"At this stage we are not planning on intervening," Gordhan said on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum (WEF).

Gordhan told SABC TV earlier on Wednesday that it was fortunate that the biggest economy in Africa was experiencing a strong currency, adding had it not been for the rand's gains, fuel and food prices would be much higher.

Like other emerging markets, strong capital inflows into South Africa in the wake of loose monetary policy in developed countries have been the main driver of the rand's gains.

Gordhan said the government was still concerned about the impact of short-term capital inflows. South Africa rejected the idea of implementing a tax on capital inflow, like other countries such as Brazil, but has opted to raise its foreign exchange reserves to limit rand gains.

Inflation has been within the central bank's target of between 3 and 6 percent since February 2010, and the central bank expects it to stay in that band until the end of 2012. It stood at 4.1 percent year-on-year in March.

South Africa's benign inflation environment has allowed the central bank to keep the repo rate steady at 5.5 percent at a time when other emerging markets are starting to tighten monetary policy.

Analysts expect South Africa to start raising interest rates only towards the end of the year, after decreasing them by 650 basis points between December 2008 and December 2010.

The rand's gains have hurt the manufacturing sector, Gordhan acknowledged. "It does have a negative impact on manufacturing," he said.

At current levels, it is considered too strong by manufacturers who would rather see it trading above 8.00 to the dollar.

The sector was the hardest hit by a recession in 2009 and although it is on a recovery, output levels are still below pre-recession levels.

Trade Minister Rob Davies, a left-leaning cabinet member, said the currency was overvalued but did not say what currency policy the government should pursue.

"The rand is overvalued due to the continued uneven nature of the world economic recovery and the policies that are being followed by some of the major players," Davies said at the WEF.

"The overvalued rand is still hitting us in the value-added sectors," he added.

With a quarter of the labour force jobless, South Africa has to balance the impact of the rand on inflation with ensuring that the currency does not strangle key sectors such as manufacturing and constrain economic growth.

(Reporting by Phumza Macanda, Peroshni Govender and Ed Cropley; Editing by Ron Askew)

text:
* Stocks drop on China rate hike

* Rand firms up as concerns over Egypt ease

* Fourth quarter jobless rate dips

By Vuyani Ndaba and Gugulakhe Lourie

JOHANNESBURG, Feb 8 (Reuters) - South African stocks inched lower for the second straight day on Tuesday but remained near 2-1/2-year highs, as a rate hike by China made it easier for investors to cash in shares after recent aggressive gains.

The rand firmed, however, as concerns over Egypt eased and dealers bet the central bank would slow the pace of intervention after weeks of aggressive dollar-buying.

The JSE Top-40 index of blue chips <.JTOPI> shed 0.02 percent to 29,616.21, while the broader All-Share index <.JALSH> was down 0.03 percent to 32,788.86.

Major losers among the Top-40 included platinum producer Lonmin , which dropped 2.8 percent to 208.50 rand, and consumer goods firm Tiger Brands , which fell 1.85 percent to 186 rand.

"Due to the Chinese hiking their rate, a bit of nervousness in the market (is) halting a short-term rally," said Wilmar Buys, a trader at FFO Securities.

China raised interest rates on Tuesday for the second time in just over six weeks in what is seen as an ongoing battle against high inflation. [ID:nTOE706030]

Shares of ArcelorMittal South Africa closed 0.41 percent lower at 85 rand. The shares tumbled more than 4 percent in the session after the company's full-year results came in well below analyst estimates. [ID::nLDE717063]

RAND GAINS

On the currency, analysts say investor concerns over Egypt have eased and the market is better absorbing the news on the political situation in the north African country.

"The market has adjusted to Egypt, and European problems are on the back burner so (investors) are looking for currencies that offer attractive (yields)," said Imran Ahmad, emerging market strategist at RBS.

At 1615 GMT, the rand <ZAR=D3> was trading at 7.1720 against the dollar, 0.86 percent stronger than its close of 7.2344 on Monday.

Ahmad added that the South African Reserve Bank might take a break from buying dollars in the market to try and stem gains on the rand.

"Perhaps (the SARB) is going to be less interventionist now given the intervention fatigue and especially given the cost of intervention."

South Africa's net gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at $44.451 billion at the end January, up more than $1 billion in a month. Analysts have said the central bank does not have the firepower to continue that rate of accumulation.

The market did not react to the fall in the jobless rate but analysts say the marginal drop bodes well for the outlook on the South African economy.

title: UPDATE 3-S.Africa wants weak rand to aid growth despite G20
text:
* "Active monetary policy interventions" to weaken rand

* Government insists plan not in conflict with G20 pledge

* Rand up nearly 30 percent vs dollar since start of 2009

* Analysts doubt authorities can easily control currency

* Finance minister to discuss growth plan on Wednesday

(Adds analysis of central bank's position, graphic)

By Wendell Roelf and Stella Mapenzauswa

CAPE TOWN, Oct 26 (Reuters) - South Africa said on Tuesday that it would weaken its rand currency to boost economic growth, threatening a deal to refrain from competitive devaluations reached by the Group of 20 major nations just three days ago.

The statement by South African presidency minister Collins Chabane appeared to mark a policy shift by President Jacob Zuma's government, which previously had resisted calls by labour unions to stimulate exports by weakening the rand <ZAR=D3>.

Chabane, describing a new long-term growth plan for South Africa, said it "entails a careful balancing of more active monetary policy interventions to achieve growth...through a more competitive exchange rate and a lower cost of capital."

The plan sees unemployment falling to 15 percent from 25.3 percent currently over the next 10 years, implying the creation of 5 million jobs during that period, the government said.

At a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers in South Korea last weekend, countries pledged to "refrain from competitive devaluations" of their currencies. As a G20 member, South Africa was party to the agreement. [ID:nTOE69M004]

A South African government spokesman insisted on Tuesday that there was no contradiction between his country's plan and the G20 pledge, which was designed to reduce the risk of a global trade war.

"We don't see our growth path in conflict with G20 pledges," Themba Maseko told Reuters.

But analysts said South Africa's plan could herald more aggressive use of both a weaker currency and low interest rates over coming years in an effort to tackle unemployment, which Zuma's government has identified as its biggest challenge. (for a graphic, click http://r.reuters.com/kat32q )

Tuesday's statement suggested "another change of the monetary policy committee's (MPC) mandate is on the way, plus more forex policy change", said Peter Attard Montalto, emerging markets economist at Nomura International in London.

"I think this is a push for more activist policy on both currency and MPC, involving new interventions and a shift of the MPC mandate to explicit growth targeting over time."

BUDGET REVIEW

Chabane did not elaborate on Tuesday on how South Africa would conduct its "monetary policy interventions", or say how much it wanted to weaken its currency.

"The minister of finance will make further pronouncements on the growth plan and possible currency foreign exchange plans on Wednesday," Maseko said.

Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan, who has himself spoken out in the past against efforts by countries to weaken their currencies, will deliver his medium-term budget review on Wednesday. [ID:nLDE69I0YK]

The rand has appreciated about 27 percent against the U.S. dollar since the start of 2009, buoyed by a flood of investor funds from sluggish developed economies into emerging markets.

Many analysts said the country would have difficulty fighting this trend. South Africa has relatively low foreign exchange reserves and relies on foreign capital inflows to plug its current account deficit, so it cannot easily copy countries such as China and Brazil, which have used forex interventions and taxes on capital flows to steer their currencies.

"South Africa is but a very small boat on a very rough sea in the currency war arena. It is beyond its capacity to steer the exchange rate of the rand directly," said Jac Laubscher, group economist at finance house Sanlam.

"Its only hope is to use its position in the G20 to promote a multilateral response to the need for currency realignment... Apart from that, any country that runs a perpetual current account deficit can hardly afford to discourage capital inflows."

CENTRAL BANK

Also, it is not clear if South Africa's central bank, which is independent of the government, would go along with any plan to weaken the rand. It might be reluctant to undertake any major campaign of currency intervention; in September it said it was accumulating foreign reserves but that the process was "costly".

Similarly, it might resist the idea of cutting interest rates to weaken the rand as its core mandate is to protect price stability. Gordhan wrote to Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus in February saying the MPC must also take into account economic growth and job creation in rate decisions, but it is unclear if the government would go as far as formally changing the mandate.

For those reasons, some analysts said the talk of currency depreciation might largely aim at satisfying the labour unions, rather than being a firm commitment to a much weaker rand.

The new plan "is much more focused on employment creation and domestic growth generation than necessarily the currency", said Leon Myburgh, sub-Saharan Africa specialist at Citi.

"It's a very broad intention and the rand is just a subset of that. It's being viewed as a tool to get to an end objective, which is ultimately employment growth. I wouldn't overstate the role of the rand within the broader statement."

The rand did not move significantly against the dollar in response to Chabane's statement on Tuesday, reflecting doubts about authorities' ability to weaken the currency any time soon.

"It's more long-term, decades type of stuff -- he has made long-term comments. The budget announcements will probably have much more direct effect on markets," said Ion de Vleeschauwer, chief dealer at Bidvest Bank. title: =DJ 2nd UPDATE: South Africa Cautions On Joining " Currency  War"
text:
(Adds detail, comment) 
 
   By Robb M. Stewart 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

JOHANNESBURG (Dow Jones)--South Africa signaled Monday it won't join countries acting to weigh on their currencies despite the growth-hampering impact of a stronger rand, saying that it looks to the upcoming meeting of the Group of 20 industrial and developing countries for a coordinated approach.

Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan cautioned Tuesday against competitive action to depress currencies, which he said may eventually lead to a trade war as countries establish barriers to protect their own economies and jobs.

Central bank Governor Gill Marcus separately said that while the rand is undoubtedly overvalued, in part due to attractive interest rates in South Africa, there is no clearcut answer to what can be done.

The rand rose to highs over two-and-a-half years against the dollar, and is up more than 27% since the start of 2009. This has sparked calls from the Congress of South African Trade Unions to force the rand lower with capital controls and further cut the Reserve Bank's benchmark interest rate, currently at 6% after a series of reductions.

"There are no clearcut or easy choices. All options involve significant costs and trade-offs, and there are no guarantees that they will work," Marcus told an investor lunch in Cape Town.

Controls on the inflow of capital have a questionable track record in reducing the amount of capital coming in or on exchange rates, while direct intervention is expensive and not always effective, Marcus said.

Brazil recently increased a tax on inflows to 4% from 2%, and last week Thailand imposed a 15% withholding tax on non-residents. Marcus said the Swiss National Bank's move to reduce purchases of euros in July has prevented the franc from rising, and recent Bank of Japan intervention amounting to trillions of yen a day had only a marginal impact on the yen.

James Lord, an emerging market analyst at Morgan Stanley in London, said the risk of capital controls being introduced in South Africa appears limited. "They are likely to continue intervening in the foreign exchange market like they have been doing, but that's not going to make a huge difference."

The central bank has steadily increased its foreign exchange reserves, including using longer-term foreign exchange swap transactions. It has no target rate for the rand.

Finance Minister Gordhan, meanwhile, urged the gathering G20 finance ministers in Seoul ahead of the key summit Nov. 11-12, to put the interests of the global economy ahead of national interests.

"What started as what appeared to be an individual problem in South Africa, Brazil, Korea, is now global," Gordhan said at a consumer goods conference in Johannesburg, adding that it was up to the "big players" to come up with a global strategy for currencies if competitive devaluation is to be avoided.

Gordhan, who called on South Africans to work together to develop an economy that can grow at 7% a year in order to create jobs and eliminate poverty, said there is a risk of a global trade war if countries act unilaterally to lower their currency.

-By Robb M. Stewart, Dow Jones Newswires; +27 11 783 7848; robb.stewart@dowjones.com

title: SCENARIOS-How can South Africa rein in the rand?
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 8 (Reuters) - South African policymakers are watching with a sense of unease as the rand continues to hit new highs against the dollar, driven by a steady flow of international funds into emerging markets.

The rand <ZAR=D3> has gained 27.5 percent since the beginning of 2009 and was last trading around 6.92 against the dollar.

Analysts see it hitting 6.50 in the near term, and that would open up the door for a rise to 6.00, a level last seen in the second quarter of 2006.

Against the euro <EURZAR=R> it is also up 27.5 percent since the beginning of 2009.

Apart from some hand-wringing and attempts to talk the rand down, the government has been unable to curb the gains, and it cannot afford to rely on hopes of coordinated action on currencies from global policymakers meeting from Friday in Washington.

South Africa's economy will pay a heavy price if the rand stays at current levels. The currency has already weighed on the manufacturing and mining sectors, key exporters whose sluggishness led to slower growth in the second quarter.

Following are some measures available to the central bank, though given the rand is one of the most heavily traded emerging market currencies with average daily turnover of $4.2 billion -- the bulk of it offshore -- none are guaranteed to work.

RESERVES BUILD-UP - likely to continue The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) has said it will continue to accumulate reserves by selling rand to buy dollars, but has baulked at the cost of 'sterilisation' -- soaking up the extra rand in the monetary system by issuing short-term debt.

While reserves have climbed steadily, the policy has had little impact, and data released this week showed the pace of reserves accumulation in September was slower than previous months. [ID:nLDE6960GA].

This more modest participation could be viewed as a go-ahead to the market to buy more rand, said Razia Khan, Head of Africa Research at Standard Chartered.

Rand Merchant Bank estimates the SARB would have to consistently buy over $500 million a month to have any meaningful long-term impact. Purchases have averaged $400 million a month so far this year.

That said, with reserves at $40.8 billion, South Africa still lags other emerging markets, suggesting the central bank will continue on this steady path.

Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan said in Washington on Thursday the SARB would have to find resources for more aggressive reserves accumulation. [nN07178683]

LONGER-TERM CURRENCY SWAPS - likely to continue

In an effort to mitigate sterilisation costs, the bank in August started using longer-term currency swaps: it buys dollars in the spot market and enters into longer-term contracts to settle them.

The bank's forward position -- which reflects its unsettled spot, forward and swap transactions -- rose to $1.1 billion in September from $504 million in August, signalling willingness to step up the fight.

In coming months this will be the gauge to watch, but even if it rises significantly, the impact on the rand is likely to be limited due to the SARB's relatively scant resources, which prevent it from taking an aggressive position.

FURTHER FX CONTROLS RELAXATION - very likely Another option is to relax the 20 percent cap on South African pension funds investing abroad, and hope the domestic money leaving the country balances out foreign inflows.

An announcement on further relaxation is widely expected at the National Treasury's medium-term budget statement on Oct 27.

"There's about 1 trillion rand in pension funds. If foreign exposure rises to 30 percent, you could have potential outflows of 100 billion rand and that should weaken the rand, but it's difficult to quantify," said Dawie Roodt, chief economist at Efficient Group.

Relaxed exchange controls would, however, only have a short-term impact because South Africa still offers better returns than developed markets.

CAPITAL CONTROLS TAX - small probability

The idea of taxing short-term capital inflows was discussed by the ruling African National Congress at a major policy conference in September -- but it went nowhere, as South Africa needs foreign capital to fund its current account deficit.

FURTHER INTEREST RATE CUTS - Likely

The bank has cut its repo rate by 600 basis points to 6.0 percent since December 2008.

The strong rand has helped keep a lid on price pressures, and consumer price inflation is at a four-year low. Any further decline will support a rate cut, and some economist are saying there is space for additional easing of about 50 basis points.

But even if the SARB cuts to 5.5 percent, that is still much more attractive for investors than the near-zero rates on offer in developed economies.

GRIN AND BEAR IT

Africa's biggest economy is in a tight spot.

Unlike its emerging market peer Brazil, which doubled its tax on capital inflows to 4 percent last week, South Africa has relatively limited reserves, making intervention a riskier business.

It is also acutely aware of the fine line between short-term 'hot' money and long-term foreign investment, and the risk of measures against the former inadvertently affecting the latter.

(Reporting by Phumza Macanda; Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: UPDATE 1-S.Africa's  fx  reserves rise at mild pace in Sept
text:
* Data suggests central bank intervention not aggressive

 * Rand remains near 2-1/2 year highs against dollar

   (Adds comment, market reaction, background)

 JOHANNESBURG, Oct 7 (Reuters) - South Africa's foreign reserves rose in September at a pace suggesting central bankintervention was not aggressive despite strong gains in the local currency, a phenomenon some emerging markets have been fighting more actively.

 The rand has gained more than 28 percent against the dollar since the start of 2009 and more than 7 percent since the beginning of this year, prompting calls from labour unions for the authorities to step in more forcefully to weaken it.

 The data showed the South Africa Reserve Bank's (SARB)  intervention to curb currency appreciation remained "relatively benign" against more aggressive action by other central banks, said Razia Khan, regional head of research for Africa at Standard Chartered.

 Net gold and foreign exchange reserves increased to $40.854 billion at the end of September from $39.178 billion in August, the central bank said in a statement posted on its website.

 "In all, (it's a) disappointing forex reserves release from South Africa, with the forward position -- which now reflects how much the SARB has been intervening ... rising only $618 million," Khan said.

 Rising tensions between emerging and developed economies over exchange rates are expected to be a hot topic at Group of Seven and International Monetary Fund meetings starting on Friday in Washington. [ID:nSGE69601R]

 Gross reserves rose to $44.069 billion from $43.133 billion the previous month, while foreign currency reserves went up $560 million to $36.025 billion. Gold reserves increased by $299 million to $5.268 billion.

 "South Africa's forex reserves will rise gradually over time, but for the market, the lack of a more aggressive interventionist stance by the SARB is likely to be seen as the green light to take dollar/rand lower," Khan said.

 The rand <ZAR=D3> hovered near 2-1/2 year highs against the greenback on Thursday, and was last at 6.8450 compared with 6.8520 before release of the data at 0600 GMT. The yield on the benchmark 2015 note <ZAR157=> was unchanged at 7.29 percent.

 The central bank however says it does not target a level for the local currency, saying it should be determined by the market.

 The bank has steadily lifted reserves over the past five years after it brought a long-standing negative position into balance in 2004, but gross reserves still lag emerging market peers.  (Reporting by Stella Mapenzauswa; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

At 0648 GMT the rand <ZAR=D3> traded at 7.29 to the dollar, 0.28 percent off Wednesday's close at 7.2695.

"Dollar/rand seems to be treading quite a tight range after lows overnight when we made it down to 7.25," said a Johannesburg trader.

On Thursday the JSE's Top-40 September futures contract <ALSIc1> was down 0.04 percent, suggesting a flat opening for the Johannesburg stock exchange at 0700 GMT.

title: FOCUS: Europe's Emerging Markets Embrace  Currency Intervention
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--Emerging markets could be set to indulge in a new era of currency interventions after Poland last week zapped the markets with a zloty-weakening sting.

Poland's apparent intervention on April 9 to pull back the zloty--its first in 10 years--shows a strong distaste for export-hampering currency strength as the global economic recovery begins to take hold, and it hints that Europe could start to mimic currency-management techniques that are common in Asia.

Russia already takes frequent action to manage the level of the ruble, but the region's freely floating currencies have generally been left to do just that: float.

Following last week's move on the zloty, however, analysts warn that further action from Poland could be on the way. It isn't alone: small-scale intervention is already suspected in South Africa, whose currency--the rand--is generally treated as though it is from one of Europe's emerging economies. The risk of a substantial hit there is growing.

"The rand is expensive. There's no question about that," said Nigel Rendell, an emerging-markets currencies analyst at The Royal Bank of Canada Capital Markets in London.

Rendell said he suspects that the South African authorities have been selling the rand frequently of late as it has nudged up to its strongest levels against the dollar since August 2008.

However, the interventions have so far been on a small scale. Now, particularly if the rand makes a fresh move higher, "I would not rule out a big sting," he said.

Analysts at Societe Generale agreed, noting that while the South African Reserve Bank has shied away from intervening in recent years, fresh comments from officials this month signal a shift in tactics.

Any move in the dollar below current levels of around ZAR7.30 to ZAR7.20 could easily attract new rand-buyers, pumping the currency swiftly higher. That, Societe Generale said, would very probably draw the central bank into the market to limit the climb.

Feeble interest rates in major economies such as the U.S., the U.K. and the euro zone have pushed investors to search for higher returns elsewhere in the past year or so, boosting the currency in South Africa, for example, with its still-high rate of 6.5%. As the global economy has recovered, investors have also moved back into risky assets, bolstering the rise in these currencies.

For Poland, that pressure became too much last week, after months in which its currency had become one of the most widely favored bets in the world for currencies investors.

The euro had plunged to a 17-month low against the zloty just over PLN3.82 before the central bank acted to slow the descent. Analysts see little chance that this intervention, or any later such moves, will do any more than slow the zloty's climb. The country's robust economy, with little if any prospect of falling interest rates, still makes the currency an attractive bet.

Still, the decision to intervene gives a sharp signal that buying the zloty is no risk-free bet, deflecting some short-term inflows.

Attention is now turning to which other countries are in line to take action on currency strength. Hungary is an unlikely candidate, because it is still in interest-rate-cutting mode, which itself limits currency gains. The Czech koruna, however, "is a possibility," said Rendell at RBC.

Intervention mightn't be the right answer to boosting exports, though. In research issued last week, Stuart Bennett, a senior strategist at French bank Credit Agricole Corporate & Investment Bank, found that euro-zone growth rather than foreign-exchange rates is the key determinant of economic strength in the region's neighboring emerging markets.

The zloty, Hungarian forint and Czech koruna are all overvalued, Bennett said, and that isn't helpful to exports. But "further appreciation should not derail these economies" as long as the euro-zone recovery remains intact.

title: S.Africa cbank reiterates no  currency  peg: report
text:
* Currency peg requires large reserves

 * Rand hits new 20-month high against dollar

 JOHANNESBURG, April 7 - South Africa's Reserve Bank has again ruled out pegging the rand against the dollar despite worries over the strength of its currency, Business Report newspaper said on Wednesday.

 Both the government and the central bank have in the last few months expressed concern that the stronger rand undermines export competitiveness and therefore economic growth, but say  the need for a stable, competitive exchange rate does not translate into fixing the currency.

 Business Report quoted Reserve Bank head of economic research Johan van den Heever as telling legislators that maintaining a currency peg required large foreign exchange reserves.

 He used the example of China, which has amassed huge volumes of foreign reserves in the process of keeping the yuan's value pegged to the dollar.

 "If you have a currency peg, then you need much (larger) foreign currency reserves," van den Heever was quoted as saying. "They (China) have accumulated foreign currency reserves on a scale that one cannot believe."

 Allies of South Africa's ruling ANC have pushed for the government to intervene to weaken the rand, saying it has hurt the manufacturing sector, now slowly recovering after its plunge last year pushed the country into recession, leading to massive job losses.

 The rand <ZAR=D3> gained about 30 percent against the dollar last year and hit a new 20-month high of 7.1950 earlier on Wednesday.

 Last month National Treasury Director General Lesetja Kganyago said South Africa needed to find ways of moderating currency volatility but fixing the rand at a set level would be hard to implement and costly.[ID:nLDE62M14K]  (Reporting by Stella Mapenzauswa; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: DJ S African  Central Bank  Deputy Governor: Won't  Intervene  On Rand
text:
JOHANNESBURG (Dow Jones)--South Africa's central bank will continue to build its reserves as conditions allow, but will maintain its policy of not intervening in foreign-exchange markets despite concerns over the strength of the rand, Deputy Governor Daniel Mminele said.

"The floating exchange-rate regime helped to cushion South Africa from more severe effects of the global crisis," Mminele said in a speech delivered in Johannesburg late Tuesday.

The appreciation in emerging-market currencies, including the rand, over recent months has largely been driven by external factors such as the depreciation of the dollar, increased global liquidity and renewed investor appetite for more risky assets, Mminele said.

"These gains, unfortunately, increase the likelihood of an uneven economic recovery," he said.

Tito Mboweni, who steps down this month after more than a decade as governor of the South African Reserve Bank, has on several occasions this year expressed concern about the effects of the strengthening rand.

The currency has weakened somewhat in recent weeks, but remains up about 18% since the start of the year against the dollar and 14% against the euro.

Mminele, who in June was appointed deputy governor by President Jacob Zuma from the start of July, said the Reserve Bank would continue with a strategy of accumulating foreign-exchange reserves when market conditions are conducive.

"Over the past year, reserves accumulation was constrained by the volatility in the foreign-exchange markets, the level of global risk aversion and cost considerations," he said. "More recently, conditions in the foreign-exchange markets have been somewhat more favorable."

title: S.Africa cbank's Mminele sees no rand  intervention
text:
* Cbank says too strong currency may cause damage

* Building reserves when can

JOHANNESBURG, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The rand remaining too strong for too long may harm the economy but South Africa would keep to its policy of not intervening to manage the currency, central bank Deputy Governor Daniel Mminele said.

The Reserve Bank will continue its strategy of building up reserves, though, when market conditions allow, he said.

The local currency <ZAR=D3> has lost ground over the past two weeks yet is still around 20 percent stronger against the dollar this year and has gained about 15 percent on the euro.

Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni and Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan have both suggested the rand is too strong.

Mminele said appreciation in emerging market currencies, including the rand, had mostly been driven by external factors, such as increased global liquidity, the depreciation of the dollar and renewed risk appetite.

"Emerging market currencies have also appreciated significantly, the rand being no exception," he said in a speech late on Tuesday.

"A currency remaining at non-competitive levels for too long might have adverse consequences for the real economy. Some countries opted to deal with currencies perceived to be too strong through a combination of verbal and actual market intervention."

The rand's strength has added to pressure on the manufacturing sector, which has been hard hit by a global downturn and helped pull Africa's biggest economy into its first recession in nearly two decades.

Mminele reiterated government policy that the country was committed to a floating exchange rate.

"Whilst the monetary and fiscal authorities in South Africa have at times expressed concern about the impact of the appreciated currency on the overall macroeconomic balance, SARB policy remains that of no intervention in the foreign exchange market with the objective of managing the currency," he said.

The bank would, however, continue with its strategy of accumulating reserves when market conditions allow. This had been constrained over the past year due to volatile markets and cost factors.

"More recently, conditions in the foreign exchange markets have been somewhat more favourable, allowing the Bank to increase its purchases of foreign exchange in a responsible manner," Mminele said. (Reporting by Gordon Bell; Editing by Matthew Tostevin)

title: S.Africa's strong rand a worry-Finmin Gordhan
text:
* Government concerned about strong rand

* Would have liked stronger intervention

By Stella Mapenzauswa

CAPETOWN, Oct 27, (Reuters) - South Africa's government is concerned about the strong rand currency and would have liked to intervene more assertively in the market through accumulating reserves, Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan said on Tuesday.

The government this week denied a media report that it planned to "freeze" the rand at a predetermined rate. The unit had fallen sharply against the dollar on the report, which increased jitters among investors worried South Africa's policies may be shifting to the left.

The rand <ZAR=D3> has gained about 25 percent against the dollar so far this year, raising concerns its impact on exporters could delay recovery from the country's first recession in 17 years.

"We are concerned about the fact that the exchange rate is as strong as it is and we wish we had the capacity to, if you like, intervene in a more assertive way than we are able to do at the moment," Gordhan told a media briefing.

"We will assist the South Africa Reserve Bank in whatever way we can to increase its current reserves from $40 billion to beyond whenever we have the capacity," he told journalists prior to presenting a medium term policy statement to parliament.

Both the government and the central bank have previously said they are happy for markets to determine the exchange rate, but the bank has traditionally taken advantage of a stronger rand to build on foreign currency reserves.

Asked if the government would have intervened to override a market determined rate had resources allowed, Gordhan said:

"Hopefully we would have bought more reserves, and hopefully we can say to you next time we have $45 billion, not $40 billion."

The rand has in the last few years however been undermined by a large current account deficit, which soared to 7.4 percent of gross domestic product in 2008.

In its policy statement on Tuesday, the Treasury said pressure on the account had eased due to declining domestic expenditure and rising savings.

It said the shortfall would fall to 5.1 percent of GDP in 2009 before rising again to 5.7 percent the following year.

"The improvement in the current account is likely to be temporary since demand for imports will rise as domestic demand recovers and inventories are rebuilt," the Treasury said.

Gordhan did not mention the report on freezing the currency, a move which would suggest a shift towards the left to appease labour union and communist allies which helped the ruling ANC party retain power in an April election.

President Jacob Zuma has made some changes to the way cabinet operates, and the resignation this week of a senior policy maker seen as one of the architects of market-friendly policies, has fuelled worries that more left-leaning officials were gaining prominence. (Editing by Michael Georgy)

title: =DJ UPDATE: S Africa Govt, Ctrl Bk Deny Plans To Fix Rand Rate
text:
(Adds central bank governor, economist comment) 


 
   By Robb M. Stewart and Katie Martin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

JOHANNESBURG (Dow JONES)--South Africa's recently created Economic Development Ministry Thursday said it isn't planning to freeze the exchange rate of the rand, and the governor of the central bank said its policy continues to be to maintain a floating exchange rate.

The comments refute an internet report that such a plan was in the works to stabilize the currency and the economy.

"It is completely unfounded," Zubeida Jaffer, spokeswoman for Economic Development Minister Ebrahim Patel, told Dow Jones Newswires. "We were completely taken by surprise" by the report, she said.

Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni said he wasn't aware of any plans to change South Africa's exchange rate policy, which is set by the National Treasury in consultation. Mboweni made the comment on national television after the monetary policy committee left the bank's benchmark repurchase rate at 7%.

The rand pulled back some 2% against the dollar in early trading as traders reacted nervously to the report on online news site Sake24.com, although the weakness was roughly in line with Europe's emerging markets currencies. At 1343 GMT, the rand had recovered to 7.4717 to the dollar from a close Wednesday at 7.4100.

"They [South Africa] did have a fixed exchange rate and they have intervened in the past, but it all ended in tears and I don't think they would go back down that route. It would be a huge step backwards," said Nigel Rendell, emerging markets currencies analyst at RBC Capital Markets in London.

Afrikaans-language Sake24, without citing sources, reported that Patel, who also is general secretary of the Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union, was to propose freezing the rand at a predetermined rate.

It said the economic development minister was working with Minister of Higher Education and Training Blade Nzimande, the general secretary of the South African Communist Party, to formulate a series of interventions to boost the country's growth rate and accelerate job creation.

President Jacob Zuma established the Ministry of Economic Development in May, a month after he was elected. The ministry's focus is on economic policymaking.

"The whole episode is symptomatic of the pressures that recession and the lack of economic progress [are] exerting on the governing coalition," Goldman Sachs analysts said in a research report.

Such concerns are a good argument to attach some risk premium to the rand, the analysts said.

The coalition includes the African National Congress, the Congress of South African Trade Unions and the South African Communist Party.

title: UPDATE 1-IMF cash boosts S.Africa net reserves
text:
* S.Africa reserves up sharply on IMF allocation

* Allocation part of global funding programme

(Adds details, background, quotes)

JOHANNESBURG, Sept 7 (Reuters) - South Africa received more than $2 billion in funds from the International Monetary Fund in August, central bank data showed on Monday, driving its net reserves up 6.49 percent to $36.922 billion.

The IMF transferred $2.166 billion to Africa's biggest economy as part of a special drawing rights equivalent of $250 billion earmarked for member countries to help deal with the global economic crisis.

The Reserve Bank said in a statement on its Web site that net reserves, known as the net liquidity position, climbed from $34.67 billion in July.

Gross reserves were at $37.953 billion in August from $35.747 billion, with foreign currency holdings leaping $2.158 billion to $34.156 billion.

"The change in gold and foreign exchange reserves was mainly due to the general allocation of SDR 1.385 billion ($2.166 billion) from the IMF, foreign exchange operations of the Bank and valuation adjustments," the central bank said.

The IMF money is allocated to member countries according to their quota, which is based on its relative size in the world economy. South Africa's quota is SDR 1.868 billion.

Analysts said the data showed the bank did not intervene in the market to boost reserves itself despite the rand currency remaining relatively strong against the dollar.

"Suffice to say that if you exclude the SDR there has been very little in terms of intervention," Gerorge Glynos, managing director of market analysts ETM, said.

The rand <ZAR=D3> was marginally weaker at 7.64 to the dollar at 0700 GMT from before the data was released, just off a 13-month high hit late on Friday.

The IMF agreed to disburse the funds after central banks in some countries pumped money into banking systems and markets to boost liquidity at the height of the financial crisis.

South Africa has not had to intervene to support local banks, which remained relatively stable through the turmoil, although the currency weakened sharply in late 2008 and equity markets fell, slowing the build up of reserves.

The central bank has been steadily building up holdings over the past 5 years after it brought a long-standing negative position into balance in 2004, but gross reserves still lag those in other emerging economies. (Reporting by Gordon Bell; editing by Patrick Graham)

text:
* Rand firmer against sliding dollar

* Local stocks rebound on miners

* Govt appoints new deputy governor

* Mboweni says no change in stance on FX intervention

* Government bonds firmer

JOHANNESBURG, June 9 (Reuters) - South Africa's rand firmed against the dollar on Tuesday after the central bank announced the appointment of a new deputy governor and as the dollar fell against other major currencies.

The market welcomed the appointment of Daniel Mminele as the new deputy governor. Mminele, who is currently an executive general manager and has been with the Bank since 1999, was seen as experienced.

"His appointment looks positive from a market perspective given that he is a strong proponent of the current monetary policy framework, including inflation targeting," said market analysts 4CAST in a note.

Local stocks rebounded, with the JSE Top-40 index <.JTOPI> of blue chips gaining 0.44 percent to 20,812.10 points, while the wider All-share index <.JALSH> rose 0.44 percent at 23,049.43 points.

The rand <ZAR=D3> firmed 0.74 percent firmer than Monday's New York close to 8.0810 against the dollar at 1540 GMT.

"Dollar weakness is what is helping the rand," said Neil Barnard, dealer at Global Trader.

The currency also firmed slightly after Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni said the bank would not act to influence the level of the currency and said the bank had not changed its stance on currency intervention.

Mboweni repeated that that the central bank would continue to try to build up its reserves when possible.

Dealers said strong gains in mining stocks aided by a weaker dollar lifted the bourse. "We see the market benefiting from a weaker dollar at the moment, particularly on the commodities side," Ferdi Heyneke, portfolio manager at Afrifocus Securities said.

Impala Platinum was the biggest gainer amongst the local blue chips, advancing 3.86 percent to 187.10 rand and diversified miner African Rainbow Minerals climbed 2.61 percent to 143.65 rand.

Gold stocks were among the top performers, led by the world's fourth-biggest gold producer Gold Fields which increased 3.52 percent to 99.12 rand and AngloGold Ashanti was up 1.60 percent to 319.53 rand as bullion price firmed while the dollar weakened against the euro.

But shares in FirstRand -- which has appointed Sizwe Nxasana, the head of its core banking unit as its new chief executive -- regained lost ground to close 0.98 percent higher to 13.44 rand.

However, Telkom shares recover lost ground to close at 0.90 percent higher to 35.90 rand, despite being rated with Vodacom as "neutral" in a research note by Nomura brokerage. Vodacom fell 1.55 percent to 54.64 rand.

South Africa's government bonds were firmer, in line with the rand. The yield on the 2015 issue <ZAR157=> was down 1 basis point to 8.425 percent and that on the 2036 note <ZAR209=> fell 3.5 basis points to 8.535 percent. (Reporting by Phumza Macanda and Pakama Ngceni; Editing by Andy Bruce)

* Russian bourses plunge before trade suspension

* Ukrainian hryvnia falls to record low, central bank seen

* Icelandic crown plunges 23 pct vs euro

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Emerging assets were hammered on Wednesday as government intervention around the world to shore up the banking sector failed to stem panic-selling by investors unnerved by the worst financial crisis in some 80 years.

Fears of a global recession roiled global markets, sending the emerging equities index <.MSCIEF> over 7 percent down to its lowest level in three years and benchmark emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> to their widest in four years.

Ukraine's PFTS stock exchange <.PFTSI><0#.PFTSI> remained suspended for a second day while Russia, one of the four biggest component economies in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, suspended share trading after steep falls in the first minutes of the session.

"Markets are down pretty much across the board. It started with equities on Wall Street and the rout continued in Asia, with central banks trying to prop up equity markets and currencies," said Nigel Rendell, senior emerging markets strategist at RBC.

"The implications for the real economy are quite severe."

By 1020 GMT, the emerging stocks index had fallen 7.27 percent to 611.19 while the emerging sovereign debt benchmark was 9 basis points wider to trade at 512 bps over U.S. Treasuries <11EMJ>.

Russia's rouble-denominated MICEX <.MCX> index fell over 14 percent in the first 35 minutes of trade before regulators imposed a two-day suspension. Its RTS index <.IRTS> slid over 11.25 percent before the exchange moved to suspend trade. [ID:nL8646384]

FUNDING PROBLEMS

Emerging currencies extended recent losses as investors continued to unwind high-yielding currencies to head for the relative safety of the Japanese yen.

"Funding for emerging market governments and corporates remains a crucial issue. As there are less U.S. dollar funds available, reflected in the surge of money market rates and spreads, local currencies have come under pressure," BNP Paribas said in a note.

Iceland's crown currency sank around 23 percent to 195.41 against the euro <EURISK=>, a day after the country set its exchange rate at 131 against the euro against the backdrop of the country's deepening banking crisis.

Iceland's central bank denied fixing the exchange rate and said the exchange rate level of 131 crowns per euro reflected its view that recent forex levels were unrealistic. [ID:nSAT005674]

The island nation is seeking a 4 billion euro ($5 billion) loan from Russia to bolster its foreign exchange reserves to help prop a banking sector that is tottering under $73 billion in external debt.

Investors also sold South Africa's rand <ZAR=> currency, which fell 4 percent to six-year lows against the dollar, further pressured by news that senior members of its ruling African National Congress party could break away from the movement. [ID:nJAT003842]

The Turkish lira <TRY=>, another bellwether emerging market, fell 2.4 percent versus the dollar while Turkey's benchmark dollar bond <TRGLB30=RR> saw its yield rise nearly 25 basis points. (Additional reporting by Carolyn Cohn; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: UPDATE 2-S.Africa cbank-inflation expectations deteriorating
text:
(Adds more Mboweni comments)

PRETORIA, May 13 (Reuters) - South Africa's central bank said on Tuesday inflation was expected to rise, but that it remained committed to bringing the gauge within target range "over a reasonable time horizon".

The targeted CPIX consumer inflation gauge has persisted above the top end of a 3-6 percent range since April 2007, and accelerated to a new five-year high of 10.1 percent year-on-year in March.

"The inflation outlook has deteriorated since the publication of the previous monetary policy review in November 2007," the central bank said in a twice-yearly monetary policy review.

"The bank's current expectation is for inflation to peak in the near term and then follow a downward trend to return to within the target range by the end of 2009."

The central bank's monetary policy committee has lifted the key repo rate by a cumulative 450 basis points to 11.5 percent since June 2006, partly to curb inflationary credit-driven consumer demand.

"The MPC remains committed to bringing inflation back to within the target range over a reasonable time horizon," the bank said in its review on Tuesday.

It said by the final quarter of 2007 there were clear signs that tighter monetary policy was beginning to impact on demand, but that the economy was faced with a number of exogenous supply-side shocks that were impacting on the inflation outlook.

"Initially, these shocks were confined to oil and food prices, but more recently electricity price developments also compounded the problems," it said.

"The possibility of further electricity price increases appears the most significant and immediate upside risk."

State power utility Eskom [ESCJ.UL], struggling to meet rising demand for electricity, has applied to the national energy regulator for a 53 percent tariff increase to help finance its recapitalisation programme. The regulator will rule on the application in June.

POSITIVE REGIONAL OUTLOOK

The Reserve Bank said a 14.2 percent increase in the electricity tariff already approved in April, the possibility of another rise and a weaker rand currency had worsened the inflation outlook.

The bank said the rand had depreciated by approximately six percent against the U.S. dollar since November 2007 and around 25 percent against the euro, the currency of South Africa's major trading partner, the euro zone.

Electricity supply constraints may also have affected investor perceptions towards South Africa and "there appears to be an increased risk premium that investors require for holding the rand", the Reserve Bank said.

In a briefing to business leaders on the review, central bank governor Tito Mbowni dismissed suggestions South Africa take steps to intervene in the currency market to keep the rand stable.

"We are not going to do anything of the sort ... The South African Reserve Bank is not in the business of managing the exchange rate, we are in the business of targeting inflation".

He said South Africa's inflation rate should be in line with those of its major trading partners, and monetary policy has to tighen due to generalised inflation pressures.

"We can't just say that the inflation problem that we are facing is only because of food and energy, it's more generalised, and therefore monetary policy has to respond to that. It's very clear that monetary policy has to tighten a bit."

In its review, the central bank said the regional economic outlook remained positive, but tensions over neighbouring Zimbabwe's disputed presidential election posed a downside risk.

Electoral officials in Zimbabwe say the main opposition candidate defeated veteran President Robert Mugabe in the March 29 election, but failed to garner enough ballots to avoid a second round vote. The opposition MDC insists that it won outright, and that Mugabe manipulated the result.

"Africa's economic outlook remains positive given the continued favourable commodity price outlook, regional macroeconomic stability, rising oil production and continued capital inflows," the Reserve Bank said.

"The most important downside risks for growth in the region would comprise heightened risk aversion by investors as a result of the tensions flowing from the Zimbabwe elections."

South Africa holds its own elections next year, but Mboweni said the new incoming government was not likely to interfere with the central bank's independence.

"I think there's a depth of leadership in South Africa which would not seek to undermine that which is in the constitution of the Republic, which says very clearly that the South African Reserve Bank ... shall pursue it's objectives freely, independently, without fear or favour."

PRETORIA, May 13 (Reuters) - South Africa's central bank did not have a responsibility to manage the exchange rate, said Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni on Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 1-SAfrica economic advisers call for rand  intervention
text:
(Adds Treasury comment paras 6-10, background)

JOHANNESBURG, May 8 (Reuters) - South Africa should be prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market to keep its currency stable and "competitive", and should maintain its inflation targets, a group advising the government said.

In its report released on Thursday, an international panel -- known as the Harvard Group -- also suggested a budget surplus of between 1 and 2 percent to help ease inflation and for exchange controls to be scrapped.

The international panel, known as the Harvard Group, were asked to assess South Africa's economic policies and propose ways to boost growth and cut unemployment.

"Maintain the current inflation targeting regime but adopt a strategy that pays more attention to the level and stability of the real exchange rate," it said.

"This involves the use of SARB (South African Reserve Bank) statements on the exchange rate when it deviates from what the bank considers compatible with external and internal balance. In addition, it (SARB) should be willing to intervene to back up its statement."

National Treasury Director-General Lesetja Kganyago said that government had long identified currency volatility as a constraint and had increased foreign exchange reserves in the past three years.

"What is new about the international panel recommendations is that it said we needed to continue to accumulate reserves more aggressively than we had done in the past."

"I would say the amount of reserves we have amassed over the past three years is quite significant, but for now... we will consider the recommendations and decide if we take them forward," he said.

South Africa brought a long-standing negative reserves position into balance early in 2004 with the elimination of its loss-making forward foreign exchange book -- historically seen as a weak point for the rand.

Net gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at $33.125 billion at the end of March.

The rand was 10 percent weaker to the dollar so far this year, but had held firm for several years after plunging to an all-time low of 13.85 in December 2001.

Kganyago said government had no control over daily currency movements. T

"What we do have control of is macro economic policy, and we believe our macro economic policy is prudent and correct."

The Treasury stressed that the report, submitted in 2007, did not reflect government views and that it had neither adopted nor rejected any of the recommendations.

Kganyago would not comment about calls from leftist quarters in the ruling ANC to relax inflation targeting.

"I cannot comment on the ruling party, but the resolutions of the ruling party are very clear: that we need to continue with the prudent macro economic policy stance for growth and poverty reduction."

Disillusioned by widespread poverty almost 14 years after the end of apartheid, communists and labour movement allies of the ANC helped Jacob Zuma win the party presidency in December, hoping he would push for more pro-poor policies.

However, Finance Minister Trevor Manuels and central bank Governor Tito Mboweni have in the past said inflation targeting was here to stay.

STICK TO GROWTH TARGET

Kganyago said the Treasury was sticking to its current economic growth forecast of 4 percent for 2008, despite signs that higher interest rates were weighing on local demand.

The SARB has raised the repo rate by 450 basis points to 11.5 percent since June 2006, to arrest CPIX inflation that has stayed above its 3 - 6 percent since April 2007.

"When we made our forecasts we took cognisance of what will be the trajectory of monetary policy and global economy ... We are sticking with (it) and will only revise it in (October)."

Consumer confidence was at a four-year low while business confidence fell to a four-and-half year low.

The manufacturing industry -- the second biggest in the economy -- shrunk by 1.1 percent in March, and analysts said it was a bad omen for economic growth this year. (Additional Reporting by Phumza Macanda, Editing by Ron Askew
