title: UPDATE 2-S.Africa cbank ends  FX  hangover from apartheid.
text:
PRETORIA, March 1 (Reuters) - South Africa's central bank ended a financial hangover from the apartheid era in February when it closed its loss-making forward forex book, enabling it to focus on building its foreign exchange reserves, it said on Monday.  

The forward book - which referred to the bank's dollar purchases on the forward foreign exchange market - peaked at an exposure of over $25 billion in 1998, when authorities used it in a vain attempt to defend the rand from speculators.  

It was created in the 1970s during apartheid era to combat economic sanctions and it has made losses running to billions of dollars.  

"Squaring off the forward book indeed represents a significant milestone and has allowed us to finally successfully deal with one of the sad consequences of an unfortunate part of this country's history," Governor Tito Mboweni told reporters.  

It has been squared off through dollar purchases from the market, which has also seen the central bank's gross gold and forex reserves rise to $8.332 billion at the end of February from $8.066 billion in January.  

The dollar purchases, which have been made possible by the strong rand, are not intended to influence the level of the exchange rate.  

"Hopefully the market will read that and say hey, these folks are okay. They are doing well. Not only do those South Africans win Oscars, but they are able as well to tidy up their books in a responsible manner," said Mboweni.  

He was referring to South African actress Charlize Theron, who on Sunday won the Oscar for best actress.  

The rand was little moved at 6.62/dollar on the widely expected announcement. "It (the closing of the forward book) opens the way for gross reserves to increase in the months ahead which should be positive for South Africa's rating with the major credit agencies," said JP Morgan economist Marisa Fassler.  

APARTHEID OVERHANG  

The forward book was originally created to allow state utilities hedge their debt on foreign exchange markets when apartheid-era sanctions made it difficult to do so, with the central bank taking on the risk on behalf of the government.  

But when sanctions tightened during the 1980s, officials at the Reserve Bank decided to use the book to defend the rand.  

After the fall of apartheid intervention rose dramatically during the 1998 global emerging market crisis, building up a huge loss-making position for the coming years as the rand continued to weaken. The forward book has been an obstacle preventing the Reserve Bank from building up its foreign exchange reserves which are considered meagre by emerging market standards.  

The large forward book, which Mboweni said was "a structural overhang from apartheid," and a then negative net open foreign currency position (NOFP), had resulted in the rand being perceived as a one-way downward bet.  

The NOFP, often described as South Africa's "overdraft in dollars" is the difference between the bank's net reserves and forward book. The negative NOFP was eliminated in May 2003.  

"With the government unable to borrow foreign currency (during apartheid), the country could only use one mechanism to raise foreign capital: providing forward cover to the private sector to ensure their use of trade credits," Mboweni said.  

Mboweni made two pledges when he became the first black governor to take the post in 1999: not to use South Africa's forex reserves for currency intervention, and to eliminate the bank's uncovered foreign exchange liabilities.  

He achieved the second goal in May last year when the NOFP became a positive rather than a negative balance. Mboweni also vowed to close the forward book, which cost the country billions of dollars, and met this objective on February 18.  

The bank earlier said that its net open foreign currency position - the difference between its net reserves and forward book - fell to $3.962 billion from $4.774 billion in January, mostly because of the treasury's prepayment of $750 million in syndicated loans.  

(Additional reporting by Ed Stoddard).

title: IMF finds no exact cause of 2001 S.Africa rand fall.
text:
WASHINGTON, Jan 9 (Reuters) - After a comprehensive study, IMF economists said they had been unable to pinpoint the cause of the South African rand's 42 percent drop in value against the U.S. dollar to a record low in the last four months of 2001.  

The unexpected fall of the rand between September and December of that year shook public confidence in government fiscal policy and threatened to push up inflation, prompting President Thabo Mbeki to appoint a commission of inquiry.  

Some policymakers blamed the fall on speculators taking short positions against the rand.  

Like the government's Myburgh Commission report issued in August 2002, the IMF economists concluded that no clear answer existed for the rapid depreciation of the rand.  

The IMF, in a paper issued late Thursday, cited a vague combination of financial market developments as a likely contributor to the rand's drop to 13.85 per dollar.  

The rand recovered all the lost ground in 2002 and is now trading at around 6.57 per dollar.  

The IMF raised questions over whether the South Africa Reserve Bank should have intervened in limiting the size of the fall.  

"Essentially, we find that financial market developments are the most likely source of the depreciation, but the exact cause remains unclear," authors Ashok Bhundia and Jan Gottschalk concluded.  

"A preliminary examination of relative policy interest rates suggest that monetary policy did not contribute directly to the depreciation, but this still leaves open the question of whether the central bank could have been more active in trying to limit the extent of the depreciation," the IMF added.  

The Myburgh commission, appointed by Mbeki, pointed to broad economic factors behind the depreciation, among them a slowdown in the global economy and declines in the current account balance in the last quarter in 2001.  

Also mentioned as a possible contributor was global risk aversion toward emerging markets, such as South Africa, following problems in Argentina and neighboring Zimbabwe.  

The commission however could not explain the speed of the depreciation nor could it find definite evidence of currency speculation.  

The IMF team said the depreciation most likely originated in South Africa.  

"It was the rand that lost in value against other currencies and not the U.S. dollar that gained in strength, indicating that the nominal disturbance originated in the South African economy," it said.  

One possible source of such a disturbance, the economists suggested, could have come from an easing in the monetary stance of the South African Reserve Bank relative to the United United States, in which case lower interest rates or an acceleration in money supply would have been the main cause of the depreciation.

title: Curtain may fall on S.Africa apartheid era  FX  tool.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Dec 5 (Reuters) - South Africa's central bank is finally in a position to close its forward book, a loss-making legacy of apartheid which has helped to prevent it building up the country's foreign exchange reserves.  

The book - which refers to the bank's dollar purchases on the forward foreign exchange market - has been steadily wound down from a peak of over $25 billion in 1998, when authorities used it in a vain attempt to defend the rand from speculators.  

Created during the apartheid era to combat economic sanctions it losses have run to billions of dollars and now its days are probably numbered.  

At the end of October the forward book stood at just $2.3 billion. There has been no update since November, the month when the Reserve Bank boosted its dollar purchases to $1 billion, but analysts say it probably stands at $1-$1.5 billion now.  

"I think the book will be closed during the first quarter of 2004," said SCMB senior economist Goolam Ballim.  

"It will mark the extermination of one of the legacies of financial mismanagement during apartheid," Ballim said, estimating the forward book at $1.25 billion now.  

Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni made two pledges when he became the first black governor to take the post in 1999: not to use South Africa's forex reserves for currency intervention, and to eliminate the bank's uncovered foreign exchange liabilities.  

He achieved the second goal in May this year, when the bank's so-called net open forward position (NOFP) - the difference between its net reserves and forward book - became a positive rather than a negative balance.  

The NOFP had been cited as the achilles heel of the volatile rand and a big obstacle to its sustained recovery, as it forced the central bank to buy dollars even as the local unit depreciated - as it has over most of the past two decades.  

Mboweni has also vowed to close the forward book, which has cost the country billions of dollars since it was set up in the 1970s. But some within the bank believe it would be prudent to keep it open, albeit at a more manageable level.  

"My feeling is they should wind it down significantly further, but not close it completely - the Reserve Bank's focus should be on building headline gold and forex reserves," Brait economist Colen Garrow said. He puts the book at $1.5 billion.  

KEY ISSUE IS BUILDING RESERVES  

South Africa's forward book was originally created to allow state utilities hedge their debt on foreign exchange markets when apartheid-era sanctions made it difficult to do so, with the central bank taking on the risk on behalf of the government.  

But when sanctions tightened during the 1980s, officials at the Reserve Bank decided to use the book to defend the rand.  

After the fall of apartheid intervention rose dramatically during the 1998 global emerging market crisis, building up a huge loss-making position for the coming years as the rand continued to weaken.  

In 2001 losses on the forward book amounted to 28 billion rand ($4.1 billion). To cover them, the Treasury said it would issue seven billion rand of zero coupon bonds to the Reserve Bank over each of the coming four years.  

Garrow said it may not have to fund that entire amount now because the rand's sustained rally over the past two years - which amounts to close to 80 percent against the dollar - may mean that the forward book is producing profits.  

But in any case, the main issue is to remove the obstacles which prevent the Reserve Bank from building South Africa's reserves, which at $7.88 billion are far behind its emerging market peers and makes the rand vulnerable to speculators.  

According to IMF data - which excludes the gold component included in South Africa's reserves - China has $384 billion, and Turkey has $33 billion. The Czech Republic - with an economy half the size of South Africa - has about $26 billion.  

Most economists say that there is no "magical number" for adequate reserves, but Bank of America's emerging market analyst Callum Henderson says $20 billion would be more reasonable.

title: S.Africa auto parts makers urge rand  intervention .
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 7 (Reuters) - South Africa's auto parts manufacturers added their voices on Tuesday to a growing chorus of calls for official intervention to stem the rampant rand, as it rocketed to new 3-1/2 year peaks against the dollar.  

This took gains this year in the volatile unit, which threatens to curb growth in South Africa's export-driven economy, to more than 26 percent. On a more important trade-weighted basis, it has appreciated by 18.5 percent.  

The executive director of the National Association of Automotive Components and Allied Manufacturers (Naacam), Clive Williams, told Reuters he was drafting a letter to the Reserve Bank which he hoped to send by the end of the week.  

"This is very serious. For the last seven years, exports grew by 40 percent. Over the past (three) quarters growth is down to five percent," he said.  

"Manufacturers are losing export contracts and at the same time they have to compete with cheap imports at home." Car parts makers are linked to automobile production, which is South Africa's biggest manufacturing industry.  

The official mandate of South Africa's independent central bank is to ensure price stability through achieving the government's three to six percent inflation target - not to manage the exchange rate of the volatile rand.  

But this has not yet filtered through to the general public, and various industry groups have recently urged the Reserve Bank to buy dollars in a bid to stem the rally in the rand, which is so far the best performing currency in 2003.  

There has so far been no comment from the government on the unit's gains this year, which has started to erode the export earnings of top companies - prompting howls of anguish - and also hit official tax revenues.  

Most of the rand's latest appreication has been driven by broad dollar weakness, although higher commodity prices and the appeal of South Africa's high interest rates to global investors have played a role, as appetite for emerging markets returns.  

The currency's trend has held despite the central bank's decision to cut its key repo rate by 350 basis points to ten percent so far this year. More rate cuts are expected, with markets pricing in another 200 basis points this year.  

"The Reserve Bank is the one driving the value of the rand through their high interest rate policy because they want to bring inflation down," Williams told Reuters.  

South Africa's targeted CPIX inflation rate rose by 6.3 percent in August, down from a peak of 11.3 percent last year but still just outside its target range.  

On foreign exchange markets, the rand surged to a new 3-1/2 year peak of 6.78 against the struggling dollar on Tuesday.  

Williams said Naacam would like to see the rand between 9.30-9.60 against the euro compared with 8.05 now, and about nine to the dollar.  

"We had started to make significant inroads into the United States. With such a weak dollar, it's difficult to compete with American manufacturers," he said.  

Naacam's latest data show the value of component exports jumped by 47.6 percent to 18.6 billion rand ($2.73 billion) in 2001 from 12.6 billion rand in 2000, with a sharp plunge in the rand that year contributing to the jump.  

Exports were forecast to rise to 24.5 billion rand in 2002, with figures due later this year.  

Catalytic converters, which make up almost 50 percent of component exports, have attracted the world's major producers of the auto exhaust system to South Africa.  

South Africa supplies about 30 percent of the EU's catalytic converters. Auto makers such as Renault (RENA.PA), Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) and Ford (F.N) and BMW (BMWG.DE) have invested in the local components industry.

title: UPDATE 1-Strong SAfrica rand no threat to ratings-agencies.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 1 (Reuters) - South Africa's robust rand may curb domestic exports, the main engine of economic growth, but it does not pose a threat to the country's investment-grade credit ratings, two top rating agencies said on Wednesday.   

 The rand's surge to three-year peaks against the broadly weaker dollar this week has fanned fears that the economy will be severely hit by its strength, with many top local firms warning that earnings will fall - possibly leading to job cuts.   

 But Standard and Poor's and Moody's told Reuters in separate interviews that the overall outlook for the country's economy remained sound, with inflation on a sustainable downward trend and government coffers still in reasonably good shape.   

 "As far as broader issues are concerned, from a credit point of view we are not worried, the fiscal picture looks reasonably robust," Conrad Reuss, S&P managing director for sovereign ratings, said in a telephone interview from London.   

 "The strong rand will not affect the rating that we have on South Africa, or the stable outlook." S&P raised its long-term foreign currency ratings for South Africa to BBB from BBB-minus in May, citing the strength of the country's finances.   

 The rand has appreciated by about 65 percent against the dollar since hitting a record low of 13.85/dollar late in 2001, making it the world's star performer in 2002 and so far in 2003.   

 It dipped to 6.87/dollar on Tuesday, its best level since September 2000. Its latest spurt has been driven by the broadly weaker greenback, with strong commodity prices and the appeal of South Africa's high interest rates to foreigners also factors.   

 The trend has prompted howls of anguish from trade unions as well as the country's top miners, which earn dollars for their exports and pay costs in rand. Importing firms may also be squeezed by hedging in anticipation of currency weakness.   

 "We are still seeing some dynamics in the export sector," Moody's Vice President and Senior Credit Officer Kristin Lindow told Reuters in a telephone interview from New York.   

 "The external position of the country is still in good shape, the current account deficit is still small - I wouldn't call for doom and gloom yet."   

 Moody's assigned South Africa a BAA2 rating for its foreign currency denominated debt in December 2001, and upgraded the outlook to positive in February 2003.   

 Finance Minister Trevor Manuel has warned that his forecast budget deficit for fiscal 2003/4 would modestly breach the 2.4 percent of gross domestic product seen in the February budget, partly because of falling corporate tax revenues.   

 LOWER INTEREST RATES TO BOOST GROWTH   

 But Reuss said that the negative impact of slowing exports - which account for 35 percent of South Africa's GDP - should be at least partially offset by lower domestic interest rates and a pickup in the global economy.   

 South Africa's central bank has slashed its key repo rate by 350 basis points to ten percent so far this year, unwinding most of the hikes it made last year to quash soaring prices ignited by the rand's historic slump late in 2001.   

 Lindow said it was not so much the level of the rand which was an issue as the uncertainty about what it was going to do next, and the fact that companies may have made plans on the basis of the currency being weaker than it is now.   

 "Companies that are thinking of going in are worried about the volatility of the exchange rate," she said.   

 "But products produced in South Africa can still be competitive at seven rand (to the dollar). The problem is that plans have been made with a different level of the rand...but who knows how long it will stay there, it could go back."   

 Both Reuss and Lindow said that it was wise for South Africa's monetary authorities to avoid intervention aimed at curbing the rand's rally, as this could backfire - as it did when the rand dived in the emerging market crisis in 1998.

title: Emerging  FX -Lira nudges up on troop optimism, rand eyes MPC.
text:
LONDON, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira edged up against the dollar on Wednesday on optimism the government and military were close to agreement on sending troops to Iraq, while the South African rand was rangy ahead of Thursday's interest rate decision. Thelira strengthened to under 1.4 million per dollar  early on with dealers finding encouragement from signs that no obvious rift emerged between military top brass and government leaders from a meeting on the troops issue on Tuesday. 

 By 0930 GMT, the lira traded at 1,400,000 to the dollar 


 
  from 1,401,500 at Tuesday's close.
 "From what we hear there's nothing negative coming out of
 these meetings...there had been concern there was going to be



some sort of opposition," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging markets analyst
at Bank of America.



Even if the military and government do agree, the matter will still
have to go through parliament, which is unlikely to be
straightforward.



Deputies' rejection of a bill to allow U.S. troops to use Turkish
facilities to prepare for an attack on neighbouring Iraq earlier this
year effectively shut the door on billions of dollars worth of U.S. aid
and loans.



The lira also found some support from reasonably well received debt
auctions on Tuesday. Optimism over the country's economic recovery
prospects brought lower-than-expected yields at Tuesday's auctions of
238-day and 406-day paper.



Evans said dealers would be nervous about pushing the lira much
stronger from current levels, given the persistent risk of central bankintervention to cap its gains.



RAND AWAITS RATE DECISION



In South Africa, the central bank's bi-monthly two-day Monetary Policy
Committee meeting got underway, with a majority of analysts expecting a
100 basis point rate cut.



However, rand dealers were treading cautiously given the considerable
risk of a deeper cut following dovish comments from bank Governor Tito
Mboweni last week.



"There is a good case for an aggressive move of at least 150 basis
points," said Razia Khan, chief Africa economist at Standard
Chartered.



"At the last MPC meeting, a majority of members were in favour of a cut
of more than 100 basis points. Since then, June inflation data has
surprised on the downside."



London dealers said the rand was twitching at the prospect of a big
cut, having already fallen back from last week's three-month highs
against the greenback.



The main repo rate currently stands at 12 percent. The rand traded a
shade lower at 7.41 to the dollar .

title: Text of speech by S.Africa c.bank governor Tito Mboweni.
text:
4. Balance of Payments: 

 The current slowdown observed in the manufacturing sector is not simply a question of a recovering exchange rate, but more significantly the weak state of global demand. South African exporters will have to focus even more on improving competitiveness through productivity enhancements. 

 The slowdown in exports, combined with a relatively buoyant import demand due to increased investment expenditure, resulted in a current account deficit of R6,8 billion (approximately 0,6 per cent of GDP) in the first quarter of 2003. This followed a surplus of R4,3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2002. The most recent trade figures, however, suggest that although the current account deficit is likely to persist in the second quarter, it is not a major cause for concern. 

 The financial account also recorded a deficit of R4,2 billion in the first quarter which reflected in part activities of non-residents in the share and bond markets. During the first quarter of this year, non-residents' total net sales of shares and bonds amounted to R7,6 billion. In the second quarter however, non-residents were net purchasers of shares and bonds amounting to R10.9 billion. 

 5. Reserves management: 

 The role of foreign reserves held by a central bank has changed considerably since the early 1970s. Under the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates, which was in place until the early 1970s, countries had to have reserves in order to maintain a fixed exchange rate. 

 Later on, many countries, including South Africa, adopted a floating exchange rate regime where reserves were used to smooth temporary fluctuations in the exchange rate. With the adoption of an inflation-targeting monetary policy framework in 2001, South Africa has abandoned the practice of aggressive intervention in the foreign exchange market with the purpose of influencing the level of the rand's exchange rate. 

 In addition, the Bank and the National Treasury made a concerted effort to eliminate the negative net open foreign currency position (NOFP) from a high of - R23,2 billion in September 1998. This goal was achieved in May 2003 and opened the way towards steadily increasing the Bank's reserves. At the same time, the Bank also streamlined its reserve management structures and processes. 

 As at 30 June 2003, the gross foreign exchange reserves of the Bank amounted to US$7.7 billion. Of this, US$6.5 billion consisted of foreign exchange, mainly US dollar, and US$1.2 billion consisted of gold. The Bank's borrowed reserves (foreign loans) amounted to US$2.9 billion. The net reserves therefore amounted to US$4.8 billion. Given the level of reserves and an oversold forward foreign exchange book to the amount of US$3.7 billion as at 30 June 2003, the positive NOFP of the Bank amounted to US$1,1 billion, with the negative position having been expunged during May 2003. 

 In managing its reserves, the Bank strives to balance three main objectives. The most important objective is to preserve the capital value of the reserves. The level of the Bank's reserves is closely monitored by the international financial community and contributes to South Africa's overall rating as a stable and safe investment destination. 

 Therefore, any erosion of the capital value of reserves will not only dent the general perception of the Bank's ability to manage its reserves, but will also harm perceptions about South Africa as a country. The second objective is to have adequate liquidity to enable the Bank to meet its day-to-day foreign exchange commitments without incurring significant penalties arising from liquidating investments. 

 The Bank needs foreign exchange on a daily basis for its own transactions and commitments to its correspondent banks, to provide to its clients, such as the National Treasury, and to manage liquidity within the domestic money market as part of its implementation of monetary policy. 

 The third objective is to earn a market related return on the Bank's gold and foreign exchange reserves within a framework of acceptable risks. Although the main objective of a central bank is not to maximise profits, it should still generate sufficient income to cover its operational costs and to facilitate the implementation monetary policy. 

 In order to balance the Bank's objectives of having adequate liquidity for its daily foreign exchange commitments and earning an acceptable return on the investment of its reserves, the foreign exchange part of the reserves was divided into two broad tranches, namely a liquidity tranche and an investment tranche. 

 The main purpose of having a liquidity tranche is to have sufficient foreign exchange available for the Bank's daily foreign exchange transactions. The size of the liquidity tranche has to be sufficient to provide for all operational requirements of the Bank, and also to enable the financing of unpredictable cash flows. 

 The stable portion of the Bank's reserves over time, that is the portion that is not required for day-to-day cash needs, was allocated to the investment tranche of the reserves. This tranche is used to increase the return on the Bank's reserves. A portion of the investment tranche is managed by a number of external fund managers and another portion is managed internally. 

 Investments are subject to conservative investment guidelines in order to limit fund managers' risk exposures, and the results are measured against pre-defined benchmarks at regular intervals. A risk-management section within the Financial Markets Department continuously monitors the returns and risk exposures of both the internally and externally managed portfolios and promptly follows up any negative deviations. 

 6. Exchange Rate Developments: 

 The behaviour of the rand continues to perplex many observers. Following the 26 per cent recovery of the nominal effective exchange rate during 2002 as a whole, the rand continued on its recovery path, albeit characterised by periodic volatility. In recent weeks the rand has remained relatively stable, and as of this morning the trade-weighted appreciation of the rand since the beginning of the year was 13,3 per cent. The behaviour of the rand has continued to confound pessimists who find little basis for the recent value of the rand. The depreciation of the rand in 2001 was clearly overdone. 

 Prior to that, there was not a general view that the rand was overvalued. If anything, the current fundamentals are now in better shape than they were at that time, so it should not be a surprise that the rand made such a significant recovery. Although there can be no doubt that interest rate differentials have played a role in the recent recovery of the rand, even market analysts are sharply divided as to the extent of this effect. 

 Although many argue that if interest rates come down lower in South Africa, the rand will retrace its value to significantly lower levels, others point to the fundamentals, and in particular commodity price developments, and argue that the rand is around 'fair value' levels. 

 It is perhaps significant that even though the recent decline in the repo rate exceeded market expectations, the rand in fact strengthened following the announcement of the rate cut. The focus of the South African Reserve Bank, however, is on the inflation target. 

 The Bank does not have a view on the appropriate value of the rand. Obviously from an inflation perspective, a stronger rand is preferable than a weaker one, as we have emphasised on numerous occasions. 

 7. Progress with employment equity at the Bank: 

 Turning to empowerment and equity issues, the Bill of Rights, as detailed in the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, has served as an incentive for transformation in all aspects of South African society. And the Bank has been sensitive to developments within the labour market since the advent of democracy in 1994. 

 By the time the Employment Equity Act was promulgated in 1998, the Bank had already begun to plan the interventions necessary to achieve employment equity. The Reserve Bank as an employer of more than 300 people is required to comply with the requirements of the Employment Equity Act, (No. 55 of 1998). The Bank has prepared its employment equity plan. 

 The objectives of the employment equity plan reflect a balance in the Bank's approach between achieving compliance with the requirements of the Act and achieving enhanced performance through embracing the spirit of equity. According to the plan by 2005 the Bank intends to have at least 50 percent black employees and 33 percent female in all categories. 

 The Bank has already attained an overall representation of 50 percent black in its workforce and has exceeded its target for female representation. 

 A special unit, the Vulindlela Unit, was formed in 2000 to oversee the employment equity process. At this time there were only three black people in general management. 

 Today the number stands at 41 - this represents a 25 percent increase in the number of blacks in general management in less than five years. The Bank has also made serious strides in the employment of female managers in the past five years. When the process of transformation was started in 1998, there were only two females in general management - now there are 19 women in general management constituting 30 percent of total managers. 

 The Bank has developed more than twenty new staff policies over the last three years to ensure the Bank keeps abreast with the pace of transformation. This refers not only to transformation in terms of race and gender, but also to the transformation of processes and systems and the way in which issues are approached in the Bank. Existing policies have also been extensively audited to rid them of discrimination. 

 But the journey has only just begun. There are many miles ahead and we cannot afford to rest. 

 8. The South African Reserve Bank's procurement approach The Bank is likewise committed to furthering the necessary objective of affirmative procurement and has made significant strides in affording previously disadvantaged individuals (PDIs) greater opportunities for involvement in contract work for the Bank. The Bank applies a targeted procurement policy which is effected through a supplier database which is maintained on the Bank's website. 

 All interested companies were invited in the year 2000 to register on the database and this registration process is ongoing. You can register your company online through the Bank's website www.reservebank.co.za("http://www.reservebank.co.za/"). Registration allows the Bank to pre-qualify companies before a request for a quotation (RFQ), a request for a proposal (RFP) or a tendering process is initiated. The Procurement Committee, which is the custodian of the Procurement Policy, is mandated to ensure that every purchase, where applicable, takes into account the imperative of affirmative procurement. 

 In pre-qualifying suppliers, the Bank has certain selection criteria, which seek to highlight the composition of the companies' Board of Directors, shareholders and the management structures. 

 In particular, the focus is on the involvement of previously disadvantaged individuals, notably women, black people, and people with disabilities. Price, ability to deliver and quality of service, are also major components of our adjudication and selection processes. Large companies that operate in the broad business sector but do not have an adequate black empowerment component, are encouraged to form joint ventures with emerging black companies in order to comply with the Bank's requirements.

title: Text of speech by S.Africa c.bank governor Tito Mboweni.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Aug 6 (Reuters) - The following is the full text of a speech by South African central bank governor Tito Mboweni, given on Wednesday at the City Press/Peoples Bank Success Club Forum, on the subject of empowerment and the South African economy. 

 Introduction: 

 Ladies and Gentlemen. Thank you for inviting me to speak at this forum. I am told that this platform often provides for robust debate and I am always pleased to participate in such debates. My remarks today will, however, probably not add as much fuel to the fire as you might have hoped. Nevertheless I am pleased to be here this evening to make a contribution to what should be an ongoing general discussion about the economy of South Africa. 

 2.Domestic Output and Expenditure: 

 South Africa's growth performance of 3 per cent in 2002 is relatively sound given the continued weakness in the international economy. However, the quarterly GDP growth rate which decreased to 1.5 per cent in the first quarter of this year from 2.4 per cent in the fourth quarter of last year confirmed a slowdown in domestic economic activity. 

 Although manufacturing production grew by 2.7 per cent between the first quarter of 2002 and the first quarter of 2003, on a quarter-on-quarter basis it fell at an annualised rate of 0,3 per cent in the first quarter of 2003. Other indicators also point to a slight slowdown in activity in certain sectors. 

 But there are indications that domestic final demand in both the government and consumer sectors remains fairly robust. A promising aspect of this is the increase in domestic capital formation in recent quarters. 

 Gross fixed capital formation increased by 8.3 per cent in the first quarter of 2003, after reaching 11.6 per cent growth in the fourth quarter of 2002. Indications are that because the capital expenditure of all tiers of government is improving, there is greater capacity for delivery, and much-needed infrastructural expenditure is now also taking place. 

 On the whole, both domestic and global improvements in growth seem to be on the horizon. 

 3.Inflation developments: 

 The depreciation of the rand during the last quarter of 2001 resulted in a surge in inflation which prevented the Bank from realising the inflation target for 2002. Fortunately CPIX inflation peaked in November last year at 11,3 per cent and there has been a significant decline, with the latest rate for June down to 6,4 per cent. 

 Although still above the target range of 3 to 6 per cent, the Bank's forecasts indicate that inflation should be within the range in the third quarter of this year and remain comfortably within the band in 2004. 

 There are a number of factors that support the outlook for a sustained reduction in inflation. Firstly, the quarter-on-quarter figures, which give a better indication of short-term trends, show that on an annualised basis CPIX decelerated from 12 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2002 to 2 per cent in the second quarter of 2003. 

 What was particularly significant was that the main driver of inflation in 2002, food price inflation, fell steeply from an annualised rate of 17,7 per cent to only 1 per cent over the same period. 

 Secondly, producer price inflation, which tends to lead consumer price inflation, has fallen from a peak of 15,4 per cent in August 2002, to 2,3 per cent. The imported component of the PPI in June was down to minus 3,4 per cent, and the domestic component was down to 4,4 per cent. 

 Thirdly, weak global growth and inflation developments mean that South Africa remains in a low inflation international environment, which will help to contain inflation domestically. 

 Finally, the improved inflation outlook is supported by other factors such as the relatively low levels of capacity utilisation, a responsible fiscal policy, lower money supply growth and the continued recovery of the rand. 

 The improvement in the inflation outlook enabled the Monetary Policy Committee to reduce interest rates by 150 basis points at its last meeting in June. The major threat seen to the inflation target is the trend in unit labour cost, which plays an important role in the inflation process in South Africa. 

 During 2002, wage settlements trended higher as inflation rose. According to the Survey of Average Monthly Earnings by Statistics South Africa, nominal remuneration per worker increased by 10,6 per cent in 2002 and by 10,0 per cent in the year to February 2003. 

 The slowdown in economy-wide productivity growth and rising nominal wage growth resulted in non-agricultural unit labour cost accelerating from a year-to-year rate of 4,1 per cent in 2001 to 7,0 per cent in 2002. 

 Our concern is that wage settlements tend to be backward-looking, particularly in the case of multi-year agreements. Wage increases that are consistently above the actual inflation rate constrain the downward movement of inflation. 

 The Bank would like to see wages and prices being set in a forward-looking manner, on the basis of the inflation rate that is expected to prevail over the period for which wages are being set. This will not only ensure a faster decline in inflation, but also a lower cost in terms of output and employment. On balance, the inflation outlook is indeed promising. 

 4. Balance of Payments: 

 The current slowdown observed in the manufacturing sector is not simply a question of a recovering exchange rate, but more significantly the weak state of global demand. South African exporters will have to focus even more on improving competitiveness through productivity enhancements. 

 The slowdown in exports, combined with a relatively buoyant import demand due to increased investment expenditure, resulted in a current account deficit of R6,8 billion (approximately 0,6 per cent of GDP) in the first quarter of 2003. This followed a surplus of R4,3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2002. The most recent trade figures, however, suggest that although the current account deficit is likely to persist in the second quarter, it is not a major cause for concern. 

 The financial account also recorded a deficit of R4,2 billion in the first quarter which reflected in part activities of non-residents in the share and bond markets. During the first quarter of this year, non-residents' total net sales of shares and bonds amounted to R7,6 billion. In the second quarter however, non-residents were net purchasers of shares and bonds amounting to R10.9 billion. 

 5. Reserves management: 

 The role of foreign reserves held by a central bank has changed considerably since the early 1970s. Under the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates, which was in place until the early 1970s, countries had to have reserves in order to maintain a fixed exchange rate. 

 Later on, many countries, including South Africa, adopted a floating exchange rate regime where reserves were used to smooth temporary fluctuations in the exchange rate. With the adoption of an inflation-targeting monetary policy framework in 2001, South Africa has abandoned the practice of aggressive intervention in the foreign exchange market with the purpose of influencing the level of the rand's exchange rate. 

 In addition, the Bank and the National Treasury made a concerted effort to eliminate the negative net open foreign currency position (NOFP) from a high of - R23,2 billion in September 1998. This goal was achieved in May 2003 and opened the way towards steadily increasing the Bank's reserves. At the same time, the Bank also streamlined its reserve management structures and processes. 

 As at 30 June 2003, the gross foreign exchange reserves of the Bank amounted to US$7.7 billion. Of this, US$6.5 billion consisted of foreign exchange, mainly US dollar, and US$1.2 billion consisted of gold. The Bank's borrowed reserves (foreign loans) amounted to US$2.9 billion. The net reserves therefore amounted to US$4.8 billion. Given the level of reserves and an oversold forward foreign exchange book to the amount of US$3.7 billion as at 30 June 2003, the positive NOFP of the Bank amounted to US$1,1 billion, with the negative position having been expunged during May 2003. 

 In managing its reserves, the Bank strives to balance three main objectives. The most important objective is to preserve the capital value of the reserves. The level of the Bank's reserves is closely monitored by the international financial community and contributes to South Africa's overall rating as a stable and safe investment destination. 

 Therefore, any erosion of the capital value of reserves will not only dent the general perception of the Bank's ability to manage its reserves, but will also harm perceptions about South Africa as a country. The second objective is to have adequate liquidity to enable the Bank to meet its day-to-day foreign exchange commitments without incurring significant penalties arising from liquidating investments. 

 The Bank needs foreign exchange on a daily basis for its own transactions and commitments to its correspondent banks, to provide to its clients, such as the National Treasury, and to manage liquidity within the domestic money market as part of its implementation of monetary policy. 

 The third objective is to earn a market related return on the Bank's gold and foreign exchange reserves within a framework of acceptable risks. Although the main objective of a central bank is not to maximise profits, it should still generate sufficient income to cover its operational costs and to facilitate the implementation monetary policy. 

 In order to balance the Bank's objectives of having adequate liquidity for its daily foreign exchange commitments and earning an acceptable return on the investment of its reserves, the foreign exchange part of the reserves was divided into two broad tranches, namely a liquidity tranche and an investment tranche. 

 The main purpose of having a liquidity tranche is to have sufficient foreign exchange available for the Bank's daily foreign exchange transactions. The size of the liquidity tranche has to be sufficient to provide for all operational requirements of the Bank, and also to enable the financing of unpredictable cash flows. 

 The stable portion of the Bank's reserves over time, that is the portion that is not required for day-to-day cash needs, was allocated to the investment tranche of the reserves. This tranche is used to increase the return on the Bank's reserves. A portion of the investment tranche is managed by a number of external fund managers and another portion is managed internally. 

 Investments are subject to conservative investment guidelines in order to limit fund managers' risk exposures, and the results are measured against pre-defined benchmarks at regular intervals. A risk-management section within the Financial Markets Department continuously monitors the returns and risk exposures of both the internally and externally managed portfolios and promptly follows up any negative deviations. 

 6. Exchange Rate Developments: 

 The behaviour of the rand continues to perplex many observers. Following the 26 per cent recovery of the nominal effective exchange rate during 2002 as a whole, the rand continued on its recovery path, albeit characterised by periodic volatility. In recent weeks the rand has remained relatively stable, and as of this morning the trade-weighted appreciation of the rand since the beginning of the year was 13,3 per cent. The behaviour of the rand has continued to confound pessimists who find little basis for the recent value of the rand. The depreciation of the rand in 2001 was clearly overdone. 

 Prior to that, there was not a general view that the rand was overvalued. If anything, the current fundamentals are now in better shape than they were at that time, so it should not be a surprise that the rand made such a significant recovery. Although there can be no doubt that interest rate differentials have played a role in the recent recovery of the rand, even market analysts are sharply divided as to the extent of this effect. 

 Although many argue that if interest rates come down lower in South Africa, the rand will retrace its value to significantly lower levels, others point to the fundamentals, and in particular commodity price developments, and argue that the rand is around 'fair value' levels. 

 It is perhaps significant that even though the recent decline in the repo rate exceeded market expectations, the rand in fact strengthened following the announcement of the rate cut. The focus of the South African Reserve Bank, however, is on the inflation target. 

 The Bank does not have a view on the appropriate value of the rand. Obviously from an inflation perspective, a stronger rand is preferable than a weaker one, as we have emphasised on numerous occasions. 

 7. Progress with employment equity at the Bank: 

 Turning to empowerment and equity issues, the Bill of Rights, as detailed in the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, has served as an incentive for transformation in all aspects of South African society. And the Bank has been sensitive to developments within the labour market since the advent of democracy in 1994. 

 By the time the Employment Equity Act was promulgated in 1998, the Bank had already begun to plan the interventions necessary to achieve employment equity. The Reserve Bank as an employer of more than 300 people is required to comply with the requirements of the Employment Equity Act, (No. 55 of 1998). The Bank has prepared its employment equity plan. 

 The objectives of the employment equity plan reflect a balance in the Bank's approach between achieving compliance with the requirements of the Act and achieving enhanced performance through embracing the spirit of equity. According to the plan by 2005 the Bank intends to have at least 50 percent black employees and 33 percent female in all categories. 

 The Bank has already attained an overall representation of 50 percent black in its workforce and has exceeded its target for female representation. 

 A special unit, the Vulindlela Unit, was formed in 2000 to oversee the employment equity process. At this time there were only three black people in general management. 

 Today the number stands at 41 - this represents a 25 percent increase in the number of blacks in general management in less than five years. The Bank has also made serious strides in the employment of female managers in the past five years. When the process of transformation was started in 1998, there were only two females in general management - now there are 19 women in general management constituting 30 percent of total managers. 

 The Bank has developed more than twenty new staff policies over the last three years to ensure the Bank keeps abreast with the pace of transformation. This refers not only to transformation in terms of race and gender, but also to the transformation of processes and systems and the way in which issues are approached in the Bank. Existing policies have also been extensively audited to rid them of discrimination. 

 But the journey has only just begun. There are many miles ahead and we cannot afford to rest.

The South African Reserve Bank's procurement approach The Bank is likewise committed to furthering the necessary objective of affirmative procurement and has made significant strides in affording previously disadvantaged individuals (PDIs) greater opportunities for involvement in contract work for the Bank. The Bank applies a targeted procurement policy which is effected through a supplier database which is maintained on the Bank's website.

Registration allows the Bank to pre-qualify companies before a request for a quotation (RFQ), a request for a proposal (RFP) or a tendering process is initiated. title: Exporters rescue S.Africa rand from 4-month low.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Export orders brought South Africa's rand back from its weakest level in four months on Wednesday, after it took a hit from political turmoil in Zimbabwe. 

 The rand was down ten cents against the dollar at 10.85 at 1410 GMT, recovering from a four month low of 10.95 earlier in the day. At this level the currency has lost 2.8 percent of its value over the last two days. 

 Dealers said Zimbabwe's eviction of white farmers and the absence of public condemnation from domestic authorities - along with worse-than-expected inflation data on Tuesday - had hurt the rand, but exporters had halted the decline. 

 "The guys were looking to take the rand past 11 to the dollar, then this export order came in," one Johannesburg-based trader said. But he said the currency would remain vulnerable to a further slide while it stayed in its current range. 

 "While it stays above 10.75-10.80, 11 (dollars) is still on the cards," he said. 

 "The feeling is that the rand will take out 11 quite soon," another trader added. 

 News that South Africa had intervened on behalf of its citizens caught up in Zimbabwe's land crisis was seen seen as a positive influence on the currency. 

 On Tuesday, a senior U.S. official said that Washington did not consider Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe a legitimate leader and was working with South Africa, Botswana and Mozambique on ways to isolate him. 

 Mugabe is pushing ahead with his government's programme to resettle landless blacks, ordering 2,900 of the country's remaining 4,500 white commercial farmers to quit their land without compensation. 

 "It is general negative sentiment (that is hurting the rand), and what is happening in Zimbabwe is having a big effect," another trader said. 

 The rand began to wobble on Tuesday after news that inflation rose more than expected in July, although unfounded rumours that a Fitch outlook upgrade for South Africa was wrong were seen as the main trigger for breaks of key levels. 

 "We've created a new range between 10.78 and 11.05 in the short term...but I don't think we will weaken dramatically again," another trader said. 

 The rand's recovery in 2002 after a historic plunge of 37 percent against the U.S. unit late last year has been curbed by a combination of regional and global concerns. It hit a record low of 13.85 on December 20. 

 South African bond yields shadowed the rand, clawing back some of the ground lost earlier in the day, traders said. 

 "The market has basically followed the rand," one trader said, adding that the interest rate curve had inverted a little further, with more buyer interest focussing on the long end of the curve. 

 Yields on the benchmark R153 due 2010 climbed 8.5 basis points to 11.46 percent, while the most traded R150 soared by 18.5 basis points to 11.515 percent. 

 Statistics South Africa said on Tuesday that the annual increase in the CPIX index targeted by the central bank for monetary policy accelerated to 9.9 percent in July from 9.8 percent in June - the fastest since its January 1997 debut. 

 Most economists remain convinced that the Reserve Bank would hold its fire on interest rates after raising them by three percentage points so far in 2002 to quash inflation ignited mainly by the rand's historic dive late last year. 

 But others believe another rate hike is becoming a real risk, particularly in light of climbing international oil prices.

title: UPDATE 1-SAfrica c.bank moves highlighted in rand inquiry.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, March 5 (Reuters) - Repeated comments from South Africa's central bank that it would not intervene to support the rand late in 2001 added to pressure on the depreciating currency, an official inquiry heard on Tuesday. 

 Rand Merchant Bank chief economist Rudolf Gouws told a commission investigating the currency's slide that he believed the central bank's stance was correct, but the fact it was publicised helped convince markets the rand was a one-way bet. 

 Gouws was replying to a question at the inquiry set up by President Thabo Mbeki to probe the reasons for the rand's unprecedented 37 percent plunge against the dollar in 2001, mainly in the last weeks of the year. 

 The rand has since recovered by more than 22 percent from a record low of 13.85 against the U.S. unit on December 20, helped by a government policy statement and capital inflows from the sale of the government's stake in mobile operator M-Cell. 

 But domestic inflation has surged in response to the depreciation, prompting the central bank to raise interest rates unexpectedly in mid-January in a move seen as likely to curb already sluggish growth in the economy. 

 "I am in support of the Reserve Bank not trying to defend at all cost a pre-determined exchange rate," Gouws said. 

 "But by saying there would be no intervention, the rand seemed more of a one-way bet, especially with other things being negative. Some form of subtle intervention, or not such a strong stressing of this (non-intervention) would have been helpful." 

 Late in November, central bank governor Tito Mboweni repeated his position that there was no target for the rand, as monetary policy is focused on the government's inflation target. 

 SENTIMENT SEEN KEY TO RAND 

 Mark Langley, former Treasury head of Credit Agricole Indosuez in Johannesburg, told the inquiry that sentiment was the most import factor driving the rand. Media coverage of the South African Reserve Bank's (SARB) stance on non-intervention had compounded the negative view of the rand, he added. 

 "The combination of sentiment, the SARB'S action of draining liquidity, and foreign fund manager activity, which can amount to billions of dollars, can weigh dramatically on the rand." 

 He said that the only entity likely to benefit from the rand's abrupt plunge would be foreign fund managers. 

 He also said the SARB's decision to absorb all of a $3 billion inflow from Anglo American's buyout of De Beers in July had deprived the market of an inflow supportive to the rand. 

 The central bank took the step to further reduce its uncovered foreign exchange liabilities - which was seen as the key obstacle to a sustained recovery in the volatile currency. 

 In his testimony, Gouws stressed it was important to see the rand's fall in the perspective of a weakening bias in the currency since 2000 and an "extraordinary confluence" of factors which began to exert themselves from September onwards. 

 Mbeki set up the probe after South African Chamber of Business chairman Kevin Wakeford alleged there had been "dubious" manipulation of the markets. 

 Gouws said factors weighing on the rand included a flight to quality assets by global investors after September 11, news of a large currency account deficit in the third quarter and a repo rate cut on September 20. 

 The government's decision to delay the partial sale of its majority stake in telecoms operator Telkom and the resulting slowdown in the unwinding of the central bank's uncovered foreign exchange liabilities were also factors, he noted. 

 Gouws also highlighted the South African Reserve Bank's decision to more rigidly enforce foreign exchange controls in mid-October, which he said had scared many foreign players away from the market, resulting in sharp falls in liquidity.

title: Emerging  FX -Poland and South Africa take centre stage.
text:
LONDON, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Poland and South Africa take centre stage in emerging markets this week with currency analysts focusing on interest rate policy and key economic indicators and forecasts. 

 The zloty was trading higher against the euro on Monday with markets cautious ahead of Tuesday's unveiling of the government's medium term economic policy programme and Wednesday's central bank interest rate decision. 

Central bank policy was also being watched in the Czech Republic where the crown was trading sideways amid wariness over the possibility of further central bank intervention to weaken the currency against the euro. 

South Africa was bracing for key inflation figures with the rand dropping back in early trading following Friday's move to seven-week highs against the dollar. 

 POLISH RATE POLICY 

 The zloty pushed up to two and a half week highs against the euro around 3.5620 , according to Reuters data, mainly as a result of broad weakness in the euro. The single currency fell to six month highs against the dollar beyond $0.8625 . 

 Attention locally, however, was firmly focused on two events later in the week. 

 On Tuesday, the government presents its medium-term economic policy programme aiming to revive Poland's flagging economic growth and curtail surging unemployment, which stood at 17.4 percent at the end of 2001. 

 Since government policy will in part determine the future strategy of the Polish central bank, analysts said the size of this week's expected interest rate move was still not clear. 

 Most, however, expected a cut of 150 basis points. 

 "I'm looking for a fairly substantial rate cut - 150 basis points. There is a possibility they could do more or even less. In other words it's not a done deal," said Juliet Sampson, currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 Even with a 150 basis point cut, Poland's interest rate differential would remain substantial compared with comparable emerging market economies. 

 In 2001, the bank cut interest rates six times to 11.5 percent. 

 "We're not anywhere near the point at which the carry on zloty positions is not attractive," said Sampson. 

 Last Wednesday, Premier Leszek Miller said the government's economic recovery package would not work without lower interest rates. 

 In the neighbouring Czech Republic, traders were cautious ahead of the central bank's policy-making board meeting on Thursday. Monetary policy will be reviewed and the bank is expected to lower both its inflation and growth outlooks. 

 Following last week's central bank intervention to prevent a further firming of the crown against the euro, markets were also reluctant to push the Czech currency further up. 

 The crown was trading at 31.85 to the euro . 

 "People are pretty nervous about intervention and the currency is trading sideways," said Jake Moore, emerging market currency analyst at Barclays Capital. 

 SOUTH AFRICAN INFLATION 

 The rand slipped back against the dollar on Monday in what analysts said was a small technical correction following a month of more or less consistent appreciation. 

 On December 21, the rand hit an all time low of 13.8100 to the dollar. On Monday it was trading at 11.5050. 

 "We had a massive collapse in the rand. The market looks like it's getting rid if its long dollar positions," said Moore. 

 December consumer price data on Tuesday and producer price data for the same month on Wednesday are being anxiously awaited to see whether further interest rate hikes are likely this year. 

 A Reuters poll on Friday predicted the benchmark CPIX index would rise by an annual rate of 6.3 percent, the same level as in November, but still above the government's three to six percent target range. 

 Bond markets were particularly sensitive to the forthcoming data but currency analysts said the rand could be affected in the event of a major suprise. 

 Elsewhere, Turkish Economy Minister Kemal Dervis said on Monday that Turkey would "do what was required" to deal with a key IMF-backed banking law prior to an IMF meeting on Feb 4 set to approve a $12-billion loan deal for the country. 

 Stocks on the main Istanbul National-100 index fell 2.1 percent to 12,600.68 points, and the lira edged down to best dollar bids of 1,344,000 on Monday. Benchmark bond yields rose to 71.05 percent from Friday's 70.72 percent.

title: UPDATE 2- Intervention  "no answer" for weak rand - Marcus.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 11 (Reuters) - South African deputy central bank governor Gill Marcus countered speculation the bank might intervene to support the weak rand saying intervention was "not an answer" to the problem. 

Intervention talk flared last week when Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni said it was an option, despite the Bank repeatedly ruling out intervention in the currency market since 1999 because of inadequate reserves. 

 "I don't think there is any question of intervention in the rand. Putting money into defending the currency is a losing streak," Marcus told a business seminar in Johannesburg on Thursday. "Intervention is not an answer." 

 Her comments boosted the rand - which has lost 18 percent versus the dollar this year on political and economic turmoil in neighbouring Zimbabwe and the contagion effect of emerging market ills - because currency traders agree that intervention would saddle South Africa's economy with extra borrowing. 

 "I agree with Marcus' sentiments. At the end of the day we don't have the reserves to defend the currency. We're too small a country," said Mike Schussler, an economist at stock broking firm Tradek. 

 "But the weaker rand gives us an advantage and exports should grow. The rand will find an automatic stabiliser. With the global economy slowing, now is not the time to have a strong rand," Schussler added. 

 The rand rose to 9.1650 against the greenback versus Wednesday's closing level of 9.18, before dipping back slightly to 9.1775 at 0922 GMT. The latest gains came after the rand cracked key overhead resistance in overnight trade. 

 "The market has taken the comments by Marcus as positive. The market doesn't need intervention, dollars will naturally flow in at certain rates," said one foreign currency trader. 

 DEPRECIATION PERVASIVE 

 Marcus said the rand was totally undervalued and that there was no reason for a lack of confidence in the currency. 

 "Currency depreciation is very pervasive and it's about the uncertainties in the world. The problem is when other currencies recover the rand doesn't quite follow," Marcus said. 

 Marcus pointed to the central bank slashing its so-called net open forward position (NOFP) - in effect a dollar overdraft built up by the bank in a vain attempt to prop up the rand - from 23 billion dollars in 1998 to 4.8 billion dollars currently. 

 The NOFP has been an obstacle to the rand's recovery because the central bank must buy dollars regularly to maintain the dollar overdraft. Mboweni said last Friday it was now small enough to get rid of. 

 Also on Friday, Mboweni said of intervention: "In the central bank fraternity...it is well known that amongst the tools at our disposal is intervention. Central banks use those tools as and when they want to," Mboweni told the finance committee of the provincial Gauteng legislature. 

 "Sometimes they do it in such a way that no one notices," he said.

title: S.Africa's Manuel says won't  intervene  in rand fall.
text:
CAPE TOWN, Sept 12 (Reuters) - South Africa's Finance Minister Trevor Manuel expressed his exasperation on Wednesday over consistent attacks on the rand, but reaffirmed that the government would not intervene to defend the currency. 

 "We don't have the kind of reserves even if we wanted to defend the currency against attack," Manuel said at a media briefing after a closed-door conference in Cape Town. 

 He added it was government's policy that the central bank would not intervene in foreign exchange markets to prop up the rand. Economists say that the strategy is a sensible one given the fact that it has seldom been effective in the past. 

 Manuel said the government should be given credit for reducing the central bank's net open forward position (NOFP), seen as the Achilles heel of the rand, from about $24 billion (in 1998) to the current $4.8 billion. 

 The NOFP is a measure of the central bank's uncovered foreign exchange exposure and is an obstacle to the currency's recovery because it means the Reserve Bank must buy regularly dollars to maintain the position. 

 Asked whether he believed the rand was undervalued Manuel replied: "We can't talk value for the currency, but we want to plead for rationality." 

 South Africa's rand has hit successive lows against key currencies in the past few weeks, taking its losses on a trade weighted basis this to almost nine percent. It has fallen by about 12 percent against the dollar since the start of 2001. 

 Manuel said he could not see any particular threat to the South African economy arising out of Tuesday's attacks on the World Trade Centre in New York and the Pentagon. 

 "The key question is what happens to oil prices," he said. 

 "No single country can insulate itself from global trends, but what we have going for us is that our exports are more diversified than they have ever been," he added. 

 Stubbornly high oil prices are seen as the main threat to the government's three to six percent inflation target introduced last year. The targeted CPIX index rose by 6.4 percent in the year to July, unchanged from June. 

 Economists also say that a sharp slowdown in the U.S. economy would take its toll on South Africa's relatively sluggish rate of growth. 

 The United States accounts for between 11 and 15 percent of South Africa's exports, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said. 

 "We will be hurt on commodity exports like steel and we might get some benefit on gold," Erwin told the same media briefing.

title: S.Africa bonds yields fall heavily, rand supported.
text:
1415 GMT - South African bonds yields fall to their lowest level since April 1998 on back of strong local institutional and bank demand prompted by change in exchange's tracker index. Rand briefly supported after another round of euro intervention by ECB and strong bond buying. 

 * Yield on benchmark R150 government bond, due 2005, falls heavily to trade at low of 12.475 pct from 12.71 pct at Friday's close. 

 * R150 last bid at 12.52 pct. 

 * R150s broke through key resistance at 12.64 pct, 12.58 pct and 12.50 pct. Hit 12.41 pct in April 1998. 

 * R153s last bid at 13.21 pct from 13.39 pct close. Interest spurred by dropping of ZAR162s out of index, traders said. 

 * Rand last bid at 7.527 to dollar from 7.53 after news of ECB intervention. Euro - the currency of South Africa's main trading partners - last at $0.8665 from $0.8632 prior to ECB move. Hit as high as $0.8730 on ECB euro buying. 

 * On crosses, at 10.83 against pound from 10.88 at opening. Bid at 6.50 vs euro from 6.51 opening. 

 * Bond yields also supported by Treasury's successful first switch auction as market puts to one side inflationary concerns, traders said. 

 * Treasury bought back 460 million rand of its R177 bond, due May 2007, for 375.369 million rand of its R157 bond, due September 2014/15/16, in its first switch auction . Bids totalled 2.06 billion rand. 

 * "The demand for longer-term debt remains marked," said one Johannesburg-based trader. 

 * Reserve Bank sold one billion rand's worth of the government's benchmark R150 bonds via a reverse repo auction at an average rate of 10.26 percent. Bank also sold 250 million rand of R186 bonds at an average reverse repo rate of 10.40 pct. 

 South Africa's debt market shone on Monday as local investors piled into government bonds while the beleaguered rand found support after the European Central Bank again intervened to prop up the sickly euro. 

 The yield on government's benchmark five-year R150 bond - which moves in an opposite direction to the price - traded as low as 12.48 percent, down from its 12.71 percent close on Friday. 

 It hit its lowest yield since April 1998 after breaking through key resistance levels at 12.58 percent, according to Reuters Graphics. Traders saw 12.38 percent as the next target. 

 Heavy buying in bonds, weaker oil prices - easing inflationary pressures - and renewed intervention by the Frankfurt-based ECB also helped support the volatile rand which pulled back some of the 24 percent it has lost against the dollar this year. 

 The rand traded as strong as 7.49 to the dollar as the euro - the currency of South Africa's major trading partners - rallied nearly a cent against the dollar after the ECB intervened for a second consecutive trading day. 

 The rand was last bid at 7.51 to the U.S. currency from 7.53 late on Friday. 

 The bond rally, which came despite inflation concerns, was partly a defensive move out of a sagging stock market but also a decisive move by local institutions and banks to compensate for a change in Johannesburg's key bond exchange index, traders said. 

 A revision in the domestic bond index prompted local traders to seek R157, due 2015, and R150 bonds to replace R162 bonds, due 2002, which have been dropped out of the Bond Exchange's tracking index. 

 "The focus has been on the R157s," said Tim Marsland, head of fixed income at ABN-Amro. 

 The R157 was last bid at 13.365 percent. 

 Investor interest in longer-term government debt was also shown in a move by the Treasury to improve domestic debt liquidity in a successful switch auction for primary dealers. 

 The switch, used by the Reserve Bank for the first time to swap debt maturing in 2007 on its R177 bond for its R157 bond, was well received by the market which bid strongly for longer-term script. 

 "The auction was a successful one. It showed demand from local institutions for the long-end of the market remains marked," said Marilyn Visser, director of fixed income at HSBC Securities in South Africa. 

 The treasury bought back 460 million rand of its R177 bond in the switch operation in exchange for 375.36 million rand of its R157 bond. Bids totalled over two billion rand . 

 Leon Myburgh at Barclays said: "The market easily absorbed the duration lengthening and that is a positive sign...The short term outlook for yields is therefore still favourable." 

 Improved debt and currency markets also helped ease market fears of the Reserve Bank tightening its monetary policy at its next monetary policy committee meeting on November 15-16. 

 The bank surprised markets last month when it announced a 25 basis point rise in its key repo rate - the first rise since the emerging markets crisis of 1998 - as a pre-emptive strike against inflationary pressures and to bolster a sagging rand. 

 "The bank is probably satisfied that the psychological effect of its rate hike has sufficiently contained the risk of secondary price effects on wages and supply contracts," said Standard Bank in a market commentary.

title: Emerging  FX -ECB euro-buying boosts Europe vs dlr.
text:
LONDON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Emerging currencies in Europe rallied strongly against the dollar on Friday, fuelled by a fresh round of European Central Bank euro-buying which propelled the single currency higher against the dollar. 

 The zloty and Czech crown both rose more than one percent against the dollar and South Africa's rand also pushed higher after the ECB intervention which sent the euro briefly up more than 1.5 cents to peaks near $0.88. 

 The stronger euro was also marked up against its emerging Europe counterparts but dealers said its gains were relatively small compared with those currencies' reaction to the retreating dollar. 

 "Emerging Europe has been strengthening generally even against the higher euro, but it is premature to start talking about a big macroeconomic impact on the basis of these fairly small moves in the euro," said one emerging market analyst. 

 A stronger euro is seen benefiting the trade competitiveness of emerging Europe as the bulk of their exports go to euro-zone countries. At the same time, a weaker dollar makes their dollar-denominated imports, particularly oil, cheaper. 

 The zloty firmed to 4.4750 to the dollar, its strongest levels since September 18. It stood at 3.9152 to the euro from early levels around 3.9250. 

 The Czech crown firmed to 39.68/71 per dollar, just short of a two-month peak it hit earlier. It stood at 34.69/72 to the euro from 34.63/38. 

 Analysts added that investor sentiment towards emerging markets was improving, giving currencies in Europe some independent strength against sharp moves in the euro. 

 "We're seeing better performance in emerging markets in general. JP Morgan's EMBI+ bond index spread over Treasuries has narrowed, stock markets are performing a bit better, conditions are becoming more supportive for emerging markets," said Jake Moore, currency strategist at Barclays Capital. 

 "But it's too early to say if this is just a temporary lull in the pressures on emerging markets." 

 ZLOTY BUOYED BY CURRENT ACCOUNT DATA 

 The zloty was already marked higher before Friday's intervention, buoyed by Poland's better-than-expected current account data for September released late on Thursday. 

 The gap came in at a tame $594 million in September as a slowing economy curbed imports and the country delayed the bulk of its foreign debt servicing costs to October, analysts said. 

 The deficit was lower than analysts' forecasts as well as the $961 million gap in August. 

 "Poland is definitely becoming more attractive but the upside may be limited because of political problems that could erupt at any point. And though the current account deficit is falling, it is still massive," said Barclay Capital's Moore. 

 The slowing economy could also see Polish interest rates - currently 19-23 percent - cut early next year which could erode support for the zloty, analysts said. 

 Data released on Friday showed Hungary's current account posted a 340 million euro deficit in September after a surplus of 176 million euros in August. 

 "The contrast is interesting between Poland and Hungary because now they look to be at opposite ends of the economic cycle," said David Lubin, emerging markets strategist at HSBC. 

 "Poland is slowing down while Hungary is showing increasing signs of overheating...In terms of relative value, it would make sense to get out of the Hungarian bond market and get into the Polish one." 

 Hungary's forint weakened to 1.98 percent above its parity rate within its 4.5 percent wide trading band after the current account data. On Thursday the forint finished at 2.09 percent above parity.

title: S.Africa rand edges weaker on euro,bonds follow.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The South African rand was trending softer in late trade on Friday, tracking the euro's dip back below $0.8700, after briefly strengthening in response to European Central Bank (ECB) Intervention. 

 The ECB's intervention pushed the euro - the currency of South Africa's main trading partners - to one-month highs near $0.88. 

 However, the rand failed to take advantage of the rising euro, with players concentrating on covering short dollar positions. 

 Traders said market scepticism over the euro's gains and disppointment over the rand's failure to break the key 7.48 level the previous day had limited the currency's reponse to the ECB intervention earlier. 

 Chartists reckon a break below 7.48 would have signalled further gains for the bruised rand. 

 By 1445 GMT the rand was bid at 7.5350/7.5450 to the dollar, but off its intraday weakest level of level 7.5650. The rand ended Thursday at 7.53. 

 "The market is a bit short of dollars and we have seen dollar demand out of London," said trader. 

 Against the euro the rand slipped to 6.5170 versus 6.4662 in late trade on Thursday. 

 The weakness in the rand took some edge of the bullish bond market with the yield on the five year benchmark R150 government bond rising to 12.70 percent from a session best level of 12.60 percent. 

 "The mid-60s is a key resistance level as the market has attempted to break through this level and failed three times since August. Today there have been two unsuccessful attempts," said Barclays Capital in afternoon notes.
