title: S. African bank official sees few ways to boost rand.
text:
MONTREAL, Oct 23 (Reuters) - A senior South African central bank official said on Monday that the rand, hovering near record lows against the U.S. dollar, had fallen victim to the greenback's strength and there was little policy makers could do to reverse the move. 

 "We have said publicly that we would not intervene," Timothy Thahane, deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of South Africa said at the start of a top level international meeting in Montreal where rich and poor countries will discuss ways to strengthen the world's financial system. He shrugged his shoulders when asked what the next step might be. 

 With the rand bid at just over 7.58 against the U.S. dollar, still near last Wednesday's record low of 7.71, Thahane said, "The situation with the rand is more of a function of the strength of the dollar than anything else." 

 Because South Africa's main trading currency is the euro, which has fallen more than 25 percent against the U.S. currency since it was launched in January 1999, and last week hit a record low, the rand has followed the euro's volatile moves. 

 Asked what South Africa's central bank might do to combat the rand's weakness Thahane declined to comment. 

 Last week, the central bank hiked its key lending rate by 25 basis points to 12.0 percent. While the move was not enough to make commercial banks follow suit, it sent a strong signal that the central bank was prepared to tighten monetary policy in a bid to slow inflationary pressures brought on by higher oil prices and the weaker rand. 

 Thahane said exchange rates were not on the agenda at this meeting when the group's finance ministers and central bankers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday.

title: INTERVIEW-S.Africa's Manuel says rand victim of strong dlr.
text:
PRAGUE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Friday that the country's battered rand had been a victim of dollar strength and played down the fallout from high oil prices on growth and interest rates. 

 Manuel, in Prague for the annual IMF/World Bank meeting, said that the South African central bank had stuck to a cautious approach when it held interest rates steady this week. 

 But he said that they would take full account of the external nature of the energy price shock and recognise that the domestic economy should not be unduly penalised. 

 "You are not going to change OECD's oil output by bumping up interest rates. You may in fact be inducing unneccessary pain on the economy on the long run," he told Reuters in an interview. 

 South Africa's central bank sets interest rate policy and enjoys constitutionally guaranteed independence. Manuel said that emphasising that its actions made a difference to the lives of ordinary South Africans contained no threat. 

 "This is not a warning. I am saying that this is a call for the Reserve Bank to make. We've given them complete instrument independence. As they take stock of the situation we would anticipate that they would evaluate all these issues," he said. 

 Manuel has recently cautioned that the country's forecast for GDP growth of three percent this year might be revised lower due to the impact of devastating floods earlier this year, which badly hurt the country's agricultural output. 

 But he declined to be more specific before publication of the government's three-year budget framework next month. 

 RAND BULLIED TO LIFETIME LOWS BY STRONG DOLLAR 

 The rand has been dragged to record lows this week but Manuel said the currency was the victim of a rampant dollar and had managed to appreciate against other commodity-based units as well as gaining against the euro. 

 "It is important to bear in mind that because our imports come largely from Europe the impact is not as bad as a stronger dollar in our exchange rate basket," he said. 

 The rand hit a lifetime low of 7.28 against the dollar this week but has advanced against the Australian and New Zealand dollars as well as against the troubled euro. 

 It closed in Johannesburg on Friday around 7.22, taking heart from central bank intervention to bolster the euro. 

South Africa's dependence on oil imports, as well as gold sales for foreign exchange earnings, has highlighted the economy's vulnerability to swings in world commodity prices, but Manuel stressed this was not a fatal dependence. 

 "What has modulated the oil price in South Africa is that there is substantial contribution from synthetic fuels and that has taken some of the sharpness from the edge of the price rises," he said. 

 Apartheid South Africa, isolated by international sanctions, was forced to develop substantial technology to secure alternative energy sources from which the nation - now under majority black rule - is now benefiting. 

 (IMF newsroom, 4202-6117-6229).

title: S.Africa c.bnk says not  intervening  in  forex  mkt.
text:
JOHANNESBURG, Sept 18 (Reuters) - South Africa's Reserve Bank said on Monday that it was not intervening in the currency market to protect the rand, which has fallen to a succession of new lows against the dollar. 

 The central bank also said that the weakness in the rand was a reflection of dollar strength rather than a fundamental problem with the local currency. 

 "We are certainly not selling dollars in defence of the rand," Bertus van Zyl, general manager of international banking at the bank told Reuters. 

 "This (rand weakness) is a reflection of dollar strength against euro and sterling," van Zyl said. 

 The rand fell one percent from levels seen on Friday to a fresh record low of 7.2720 to the dollar, taking its slide against the U.S. unit this year to 17 percent. 

 Reserve Bank governor Tito Mboweni has repeatedly said it would not make sense for the central bank to use its limited foreign currency reserves to defend the rand, a policy which economists say has helped support the currency this year.
